Inquiries of the Ministry EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, I think it would be appropriate today, with General Gruenther here, for the Secretary of State for External Affairs to bring the house and the country up to date on the Geneva conference.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As I promised to do yesterday, Mr. Speaker, I am in a position to make a very brief report on the Geneva conference. The Korean talks at this conference, that is the Korean side of the conference, have made very little progress since my report to the house two weeks ago today, on May 28. It will be recalled at that time the conference had before it proposals put forward by the North Korean delegation in the earlier days of the conference, and a set of proposals submitted by the South Korean delegation on May 22. The distance between the two sides, as exemplified by these proposals, is still very great, and nothing in the nature of detailed negotiations has yet been possible.
On June 5, Mr. Molotov, the leader of the Soviet delegation, submitted to the conference a five point resolution on what he called the fundamental principles for a Korean settlement on which he sought the agreement of the conference. At first glance these proposals seemed to be plausible enough. In fact, some of them are merely a restatement of principles on which agreement had already been reached through the armistice arrangements and at the Berlin conference of foreign ministers last February. The Molotov proposals are, however, cast in such broad and general terms that they completely gloss over the differences between ourselves and the communists on this subject, and their acceptance would convey a completely false impression that real progress had been made and that something substantial had been agreed upon, which is not the case.
For instance, the Molotov resolution calls for an international commission to supervise the holding of elections, which on the face of it seems acceptable enough. But the same proposal on this particular subject would leave for later discussion the composition of this commission, and the composition of such a commission is, of course, a fundamental matter. In the light of the experience of the neutral nations supervisory commission in Korea, it would be folly to accept a commission which would include communist representatives who would be in a position to hamstring any effective supervision of the election. That, Mr. Speaker, is only one of

the questions which must be answered before these latest and very general communist proposals for a settlement can be considered as even a basis for negotiation. There is no reason to believe that the answers will be satisfactory.
This Korean conference has been going on now for more than six weeks, and if we do not get some satisfactory answers soon from the communists on the matter of free elections, and all that that term implies, and if the communists are not prepared to agree to international supervision of an election by a workable commission acceptable to the United Nations and composed of genuine neutrals, the United Nations side may shortly have to consider whether it is worth while continuing this effort at Geneva to reach agreement for the peaceful unification of Korea. If the Geneva conference fails in this task we would anticipate that the United Nations will pursue the objective of the unification of Korea by peaceful means. The Canadian government, and I am sure this house, would continue to support those efforts.
I should emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that the failure of the Geneva conference should not mean, of course, in Korea a resumption of hostilities, nor would it impose on us any obligation, direct or indirect, to participate in any action to unify Korea by force. We should, I think, be clear on that latter point.
So far as the Indo-Chinese side of the conference is concerned, the delegations who are participating in this part of the conference have been dealing with three main problems: First, a cease-fire in Indo-China; second, a political settlement; and third, guarantees of supervisory arrangements for those first two. Discussions of the last fortnight have revealed many stumbling blocks concerning all three. The western powers at Geneva have agreed that a cease-fire and political settlement are necessary, but to be effective they must be accompanied by supervisory guarantees; and, provided the supervisory guarantees existed, the cease-fire need not await the political settlement which inevitably would take longer to achieve. Furthermore, as Laos and Cambodia are separate countries, where different political and military conditions prevail, they should, in the opinion of the western side, be dealt with separately.
Since I last reported to the house, the military representatives of the two opposing high commands have met, and indeed are now meeting in camera in Geneva, in order to discuss cease-fire arrangements; but the results of their deliberations are not known. Regarding neutral supervision the communists, as in the case of Korea, have insisted

on a commission of four with two communist states plus Pakistan and India as members, a replica in form of the neutral nations supervisory commission in Korea. These proposals are considered unsatisfactory by the western powers concerned on the ground that Czechoslovakia and Poland are not really neutrals, and that a two-sided arrangement of this kind would merely result in a stalemate. We know that from experience.
The western side have proposed a genuinely neutral and Asian commission consisting of India, Pakistan, Burma, Ceylon and Indonesia. The communists, however, have not accepted this proposal and have rejected any form of United Nations supervision.
As hon. members will see, therefore, neither on the Korean nor on the Indo-Chinese issue is the outlook such as to give much hope of a will to achieve a reasonable settlement on the communist side. On the western side the feeling seems to be growing that no useful, and indeed some harmful, purpose would be served by prolonging and continuing the conference, once it has been made clear that the communists are using it not to bring about an end of the fighting but to pursue their own political and propaganda aims. I do not think, Mr. Speaker, any reasonable person could quarrel with that view.

May I just say one word, Mr. Speaker, in reference to the latter part of my hon. friend's remarks? If negotiations can no longer be continued with any hope whatever of achieving anything other than continued propaganda in Geneva, I believe there will be general agreement amongst Canadians with that stand. I should like to ask the minister one supplementary question arising out of his earlier remarks regarding Korea. He said that, in the event that no settlement was arrived at and measures were taken by the United Nations for the unification of Korea, there would be no accepted responsibility on the part of Canada to participate. What then has the minister in mind, in so far as the Canadian troops who are in Korea are concerned? What would be their disposition in that event?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, that is a question that is difficult for me to answer. If the situation in Korea is prolonged indefinitely, and if the United Nations has made another effort to bring about a peaceful unification of the country and has failed, and there seems to be no immediate possibility of progress in that field-I am putting this forward as a hypothetical situation-then, of course, the indefinite retention of United Nations forces, including Canadian forces, in Korea would have to be reconsidered.
Inquiries of the Ministry
May I ask the minister a supplementary question? What is the position now with regard to the setting up of a defence pact in the Pacific?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I can only answer that by saying that this matter is under consideration by the governments particularly concerned. I take it my hon. friend is not referring to a security pact in the Pacific generally, but to the southeast Asian security pact. There have been, as I understand it, no discussions among the countries particularly concerned with that particular issue-no formal discussions up to the present time. But I am sure that the matter is being considered by those governments.

Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege I do wish to refer to a statement made last night in the House of Commons. I was absent, as were a number of members of the government, taking advantage of an opportunity to hear our guest in the House of Commons this morning. That was my reason for being absent.
I find, as recorded at page 5817 of Hansard in replying to a question about representatives of the Labour-Progressive party having time on the radio, that the minister responsible said that this was done by the full agreement of political parties in the house. May I say most emphatically that the reason the Labour-Progressive party have the opportunity to speak on the radio is entirely the responsibility of the government and of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.

Supply-Transport SUPPLY
The house in committee of supply, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
444. St. Lawrence seaway surveys, investigations and design (including the former St. Lawrence ship canal surveys and investigations), $820,180.

Mr. Chairman, I have been informed that the minister has had an interview this week with the premier of Quebec, if my information is correct. Has there been any discussion about power development near Montreal?
Hon Lionel Chevrier (Minister of Transport): Yes, Mr. Chairman, I have had discussions with the premier of Quebec. Those discussions were held on Wednesday of this week, and had to do with the development of power in the Lachine section. As a matter of fact, following the decision which was given recently by the supreme court of the United States, I thought it advisable that there should be discussions, or at least that an interview should be sought with the premier of Quebec.
This was done, and the interview was, I think, a satisfactory one. I am pleased to be able to say that the views of the premier of Quebec on the general subject of the St. Lawrence seaway are favourable. I think he feels that the arguments which heretofore had prevailed against it, in so far as the province of Quebec-or, perhaps, the city of Montreal-was concerned, no longer obtain. He, I believe, and his government as well, feel that the development of the St. Lawrence seaway is a good thing for Canada.
The object of my going there was to ascertain if it was possible to enter into more detailed negotiations with reference to a joint power and navigation development in the Lachine section. While I would not like to go any further than that at this time, I think it will be possible to do that. In fact, I hope that it will be possible to have technical discussions, or discussions on a technical level, between the officers of the Department of Transport and those of the Quebec Hydro Electric Power Commission, leading toward a consideration of a joint power and navigation development in the Lachine section of the St. Lawrence seaway.
Are any outside or private engineering firms engaged in making the engineering plans on the St. Lawrence?
Yes.

Would the
minister give us the names?
fMr. Drew.]

I do not know that I can give the names. Perhaps I had better answer the question in this way, that we have engaged a number of consulting firms to assist in studies arising out of the development of the seaway, particularly the Lachine section. There are problems-pretty important ones-having to do with the bridges in the Montreal area, and it has been necessary to consult a number of firms. One of the consulting engineers is Mr. P. L. Pratley, an outstanding bridge engineer in the city of Montreal, whose services we sought on former occasions in connection with other public projects. And I believe we have also sought the consulting assistance of the firm of Surveyer, Nenniger and Chenevert. Those are the two which come to my mind.
Would it be possible for the minister to give us the other names later on?
Yes.
We would like to have the names of those who are engaged in that engineering and technical work.
Do I understand the hon. member wishes to have the names of the independent engineers?
Yes, the independent engineers who were consulted and who are doing technical work as well as planning with respect to the St. Lawrence.
I shall be glad to get that, yes.

The minister may recall that I have referred to the general ice conditions in the winter, and as to what has been planned by way of keeping the St. Lawrence open. I have mentioned that down east we are quite concerned about this matter. I would like to hear from the minister if there has been any engineering investigation into the possibility of keeping the St. Lawrence open all winter long, when the seaway becomes a reality.

I can tell my hon. friend that I cannot see any possibility of keeping the St. Lawrence route open during twelve months of the year. Certainly there is nothing envisaged in the plans for the development of the seaway, either jointly or separately, in connection with power and navigation, which would have anything to do with that subject either directly or indirectly. I do not foresee that in the immediate future, unless it be by atomic power, with which I am not competent to deal, there is any possibility of a longer season of navigation on the St. Lawrence. The only reason why

icebreakers are being used, as my hon. friend knows, is for protection in the Montreal area on both sides of the channel against flooding in the spring.

Have any engineering reports or any engineering statements ever been made in this regard in any of the various investigations in connection with the seaway? The reason I ask that, Mr. Chairman, is, as I explained, that we are worried about this business. I have read articles that when the St. Lawrence seaway becomes a reality-and an enormous investment is involved-it is possible that special ships with thick plates will be used on the great lakes to go up and down the St. Lawrence after the icebreakers have broken the ice. I know that at the present time you cannot take ships into the St. Lawrence through the fresh water ice that comes down the Saguenay and other rivers, but I do suggest that special ships with thick plates could go up and down the St. Lawrence. The only thing I want to know is whether the engineers have looked into this matter in any way.
There are certainly no reports from my engineers on that subject.

When I receive the names of the engineering Arms, may I also be given the ones who were engaged last year? I notice that $512,000 was allotted last year. What arrangements have been made with the United States government in regard to the seaway canal and in regard to payments and co-operation? What portion is Canada going to pay?

That is a pretty broad and difficult question to answer. I do not think I should attempt to answer it at this stage. As my hon. friend knows, it was only on Monday of this week that the last obstacle was removed by the judgment of the supreme court of the United States. From now on I take it that negotiations will be entered into between representatives of Canada and of the United States to deal with the matter. Until those negotiations begin I do not think I should make any statement, particularly if I am to be a member of the negotiating team. I would not want to tie my hands by anything that I would say here, and I do not think the committee would want me to do that either.

You have
already started to get together on it, have you?

Yes; we have received a note from the United States government, and a note in reply is being prepared now, and talks will take place very early.
Supply-Transport

Where will those
talks take place?
Either in Washington or in Ottawa.
Why not nearer to the St. Lawrence canal?
What difference does it make?
A lot of difference.
It is a long canal.

Owing to the unemployment situation which exists at the present time and on account of the extraordinary unemployment situation in the shipbuilding industry and the effect of that on the valuable shipyards of Canada, which may lose permanently skilled men who are capable of building as fine a ship as can be built anywhere, I should like to say a few words. It does not meet the situation to say that these men who are laid off are on unemployment insurance. Many of them have to go away from their homes to seek employment in other fields. Just think what a great loss it will be if this condition continues very long. These men are being taken out of the industry and we will not be able to get them back when needed, as they were in the first and second world wars. This country should have a law that no foreign boats could ply up and down the great lakes, as two boats did last year from Port Arthur to my home town of Collingwood. They were of foreign registry, had foreign skippers and foreign crews. They were operating under wages far less than the sailors' union of this country permit. The conditions under which those boats operated would not be tolerated by the sailors' union of this country. They did that for two years.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is bringing up a very interesting subject, but in my opinion it is not one that should be discussed under item 444, which deals with St. Lawrence seaway surveys, investigations and design.
This is of vital importance to your town of Midland, Mr. Chairman, where there are seven watchmen on the yard.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
In applying the rules of the house I am afraid I cannot take regard of any personal considerations, and I still must say that a discussion of this kind, in my opinion, is out of order on item 444.

Supply-Transport
Does the fact that the item deals with work leading to the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway not justify the hon. member in raising this question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member was proceeding to make remarks with regard to the use of the upper lakes by certain steamships, and I do not see how I can possibly find that it is in order under item 444.

I am sorry if I deviated when I should not have. I was trying to make a point. May I say to the minister, if there was a law in this country preventing any foreign ships from travelling up and down our coastal waters-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member misunderstood me. I cannot find that that type of discussion is relevant under item 444.

Mr. Chairman, it is leading up to the St. Lawrence waterway. May I say this? Outside ships come up the St. Lawrence waterway-I say it in a kindly way-and take a great deal of shipping from the shipping companies of this country. Ship owners and Canadian sailors are going to suffer. These ships are going to come from foreign ports and go up to the head of the lakes, load cargoes and unload them in Toronto. Is this not an appropriate and opportune time, before the St. Lawrence is deepened, to pass a law to prohibit any coastal freighting back and forth in ships other than those that are built in shipyards in Canada? I know that this has been discussed time and time again. I know how the minister feels regarding the matter. I think this would be an opportune time for the minister to give relief, if relief can be given to the shipyards, through government action. I should like the minister to announce that now.

If my hon. friend is referring to coastal restrictions-and I presume he is-I agree with him fully that this is an opportune time to give careful study to this whole problem.
As I indicated when we were discussing the first item, I think in answer to the contribution made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, this is a most difficult and complex problem, and I said it was my intention, before the end of the session, to make a statement on the matter. Unfortunately, it has not been possible for me to do that yet because of a number of features, but I do hope that it still will be possible for me or the Prime Minister to make a complete statement on the whole subject of coastal restrictions generally, and having in mind the
[The Chairman.]
great lakes-St. Lawrence seaway development, which I am sure will meet with the approval of the house.
I wish to thank the minister for his reply.

May I remind you, Mr. Chairman, that we are discussing the following item:
St. Lawrence seaway surveys, investigations and design (including the former St. Lawrence ship canal surveys and investigations).
The construction of the St. Lawrence seaway is very vital to a great many provinces. If you are going to permit a wide open discussion I should like to bring in wheat; if you are going to allow a wide open discussion there are other matters I should like to bring in. I should like your ruling as to whether we are to have a wide open discussion again or are we going to confine ourselves to item 444.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As I indicated when I rose before, item 444 deals with expenditures in connection with the seaway, and if we are to make any progress I think I must do my best to see that the discussion is relevant to the item under consideration.

Mr. Chairman, is the minister in a position to give us any information as to the probable water level of the St. Lawrence river? This will have a direct bearing on the municipalities of St. Lambert, Montreal south, and Mackayville, particularly if there is any change in the water level of the St. Lawrence river.

Mr. Chairman, the question of the water level would depend on whether the Lachine section-and I presume that is the section in which my hon. friend is interested-is developed separately for navigation or jointly for navigation and power, and until that has been determined I think I would simply be confusing the question by attempting to deal with it. This matter, as I indicated earlier, is still under discussion.
Could the minister tell me when this question will be settled?

Mr. Chairman, that is a rather difficult question to answer. I can say that if we proceeded jointly with the province of Quebec we should have to determine this fairly soon because it is urgent that we know whether we shall proceed alone on navigation, or jointly with the province of Quebec on navigation and power. I communicated with the premier of the province who agreed that the matter should be determined in the near future. I hope it will be soon.

Mr. Chairman, I think it might facilitate the progress of the work of the committee if we considered the supplementary estimates together with the items on the main estimates which have to do with the same vote. For example, on this vote there is supplementary estimate No. 735 and I see no reason why we could not cover both in our discussion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is that agreeable to the committee?
Agreed.

In the details on these two votes we find that there is a very large sum included for professional and special services. In the vote in the main estimates the figure is $473,400 and in the supplementary estimates it is $255,000. In other words, about $750,000 is involved. The minister explained earlier in the discussion that engineers have been retained. I would ask him to explain whether all this money is to be spent for engineers, or in what manner it is to be expended. It seems a very large sum for professional and special services, and that amount, of course, is over and above any work done by the minister's own department.

Mr. Chairman, dealing with the present vote, that is the vote under consideration, there is an amount of $820,000 of which $473,000 is for professional and special services. That amount of $473,000 is broken down as follows: investigations to locate a suitable area for concrete aggregates in the St. Lawrence river basin, $120,000. In effect that is to cover core drilling. Along the international rapids section and the Lachine section we have a group of drillers who are attempting to find out what is beneath the crust surface and rock, and these drillers are also performing services in the La Prairie basin.

What firms are doing this
work?

This work is being done by employees of the department, both casual labourers and experienced men. Drillers have been employed from the northern parts of Ontario all of whom are skilled in operations of this kind, and additional casual help has been taken on.
Is this work being done with government tugs?

This work is being done on land, not in the water. The breakdown continues: field services in the St. Lawrence river basin, $125,000; special surface investigation in the St. Lawrence river basin, $50,000. Then
Supply-Transport
a hydraulic model is being constructed by the national research council of the international section in order to ascertain just what effect the works will have when they are completed. That will be determined when this hydraulic model has been set up, and on big jobs this is a normal practice.
How much will that cost?
Eighty thousand dollars.
Is all this work being done by the government?

All the work I have detailed is being done by the government. The house will remember that the international joint commission, when it approved the application of Ontario and the state of New York, recommended an arrangement covering two boards. One was the St. Lawrence joint board of engineers, and there was the control board. The board of engineers was to supervise and control the power works and that board has been appointed. Then the control board has to do with the level of the waters. Now, there is $504,000 which has been set aside in the supplementary estimates for this purpose. Then there is $255,000 for professional services. These costs are additional to the costs I have already mentioned which were foreseen in the development and planning of the entire project, including field surveys in the St. Lawrence river; the hydraulic model construction through arrangement with the national research council; subsurface investigations in co-operation with the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys; consulting services; and aerial surveys.
Is all that work being done by the government or is some of it being contracted out?
None of this is under contract. This is all being done by the special projects branch of the Department of Transport which has its head office in the city of Montreal.
Then this vote for professional and special services really covers government salaries.
No.

It seems to me the minister must be wrong. I can quite understand that the item in the supplementary estimates covering $504,032 could be for paying government employees, but this item of $255,000 in the supplementary estimates for professional and special services would, I imagine, be paid out to some outside firms for that work.

S up p ly-Transport

I was going to interrupt the hon. member, Mr. Chairman, and say that in answer to the hon. member for Peterborough I indicated that some consulting engineers had been employed. They are not government employees, of course. Let us take, for instance, the firm of Mr. Pratley. He is being engaged to give advice to the special projects branch of the Department of Transport in connection with the effect which the navigational features of the Lachine section would have on the Jacques Cartier bridge. Likewise, another firm are being engaged for the same purpose with reference to the Mercier bridge. The firm of Surveyer, Nenniger and Chenevert are also being engaged with reference to the Victoria bridge. I understand they will be paid under the supplementary vote. Those are studies which are likely to take some time. But over and above this work, I think I am safe in saying that all the work is being done by the special projects branch of the Department of Transport.
Mr. Chairman-
I should like to ask a further question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On the same matter?
Yes.

I am sorry to break up this conversation but there are a few more of us in the house. The point I am interested in, Mr. Chairman, is this. The supplementary estimate and the regular estimate indicate that the money now being voted is for surveys, investigations and design of the St. Lawrence seaway. The bill that authorized the government to go ahead with this project was entitled the "St. Lawrence Seaway Authority". When the estimates came in this time I assumed that there would be set up in the Department of Transport a separate section that would be known as the St. Lawrence seaway authority or that a separate organization apart from the Department of Transport would be set up to carry on this project. What I am going to inquire of the minister is this. Is this project to be carried on merely as another departmental function within the Department of Transport or is it the intention of the government to set up that seaway authority separate and apart from the Department of Transport?
In my judgment, this is not a routine government project; but if it is going to be carried on merely within the confines of the Department of Transport, and just as another section of it, in my judgment the government is going to run into the same

kind of thing as the Ontario government has run into in connection with highways. This is something bigger than that matter. In my opinion, it is too big to be handled by just the routine people in the Department of Transport. If it is going to be done in that way, it sounds to me like Molotov's proposal to the Geneva conference: You accept the principle, and you go ahead and appoint those who are going to administer it later on.
I have my own opinion on this subject. I want to tell hon. members who are now quibbling about the details that they are just two years too late. I did the quibbling about details two years ago when the authority was set up. By the unanimous vote of the House of Commons, with one exception, the government now has the authority to go ahead with this project. Many of the members are going to be shocked before this project is completed. Will the minister now tell me whether it is the intention of the government to set up a special organization as designated by the bill that gave them authority to go ahead with the project? Will that project be taken out of routine circles as far as the Department of Transport is concerned? I think it should be taken out of routine circles. However, the estimates at this time do not indicate that procedure. The estimate at this time is merely the routine estimate of the Department of Transport to carry on surveys and investigations necessary for this St. Lawrence project.

My hon. friend is quite right in his summing up and his explanation of this position. There is no intention of building the great lakes-St. Lawrence seaway other than in accordance with the terms of the St. Lawrence seaway authority. It has not been possible to establish the seaway authority-in fact it would have been inadvisable to establish it-and to proceed with the construction until such time as all the obstacles had been cleared away. In fact, from the statements made by the Prime Minister and others, it was clear that that was something which could not be done until Monday of this week, because the last obstacle was cleared away only on Monday of this week when the United States supreme court decided to refuse the appeal. Pending that clearing away of obstacles, what we did was to establish in the Department of Transport a special projects branch that had to do with this project. When the government decides to establish the seaway authority, I believe that the corporation will have that special projects branch as a nucleus to proceed.
It is the St. Lawrence seaway authority that will undertake this project. The seaway

will not be built by a division of the Department of Transport, although the seaway authority will, I assume, be responsible to the Minister of Transport who, in turn, will be responsible to the House of Commons. However, my hon. friend is quite right. There is no intention of proceeding with a project of this tremendous nature by means of this vote. The machinery will ultimately take the form of the St. Lawrence seaway authority.

Can the minister tell the committee whether United States participation in the seaway is contingent upon the construction of the canals in the international section on United States territory? If that is so, does it mean that use will be made of United States labour exclusively? Also, will control of that section be vested in a United States authority?

Those are questions which I cannot answer at this stage, nor would I attempt to do so. I do not know whether or not my hon. friend was in the chamber earlier -when the hon. member for Peterborough asked the same question. I then indicated to him that negotiations would begin soon with the United States government and that I did not think I should attempt to tie the hands of the Canadian government by any statement on that matter. I am sorry that I cannot help my hon. friend, but I am sure that he will understand the situation at the moment.

I have seen some public statements to the effect that now the last obstacle has been removed with regard to the participation of the United States, the Canadian government was willing to have the Americans participate provided there were not any further undue delays. I wonder whether the minister is able to give us any indication of just what is meant by those "undue delays" or how much longer we must wait before we can actually put some of our unemployed to work on the St. Lawrence seaway?

I think the statements having reference to undue delays which the Prime Minister made on more than one occasion in the house had to do with the act which was before congress and the appeal which was before the supreme court. Now that both of those obstacles have been removed I would think there may not be any further undue delays. By that I mean that the governments now should get together and decide upon what basis the works are going to proceed.

Mr. Chairman, I think this is probably the right item under which to ask this question, and I should like to have the minister answer it. In making the surveys with respect to the seaway I assume that in the over-all picture the question of lake levels has been studied intensively. I should like the minister to indicate whether in the over-all project there will be further control at different parts of the seaway in order that lake levels can be reduced and held at a particular level. Would the minister also say what attitude the government is going to take with respect to the diversion of water through the Chicago drainage scheme and to what extent that is going to affect lake levels? He might indicate how soon lake levels will be reduced, what lake levels are going to be reduced, to what extent, and at what level it is expected they will be held.
I would imagine that the government is also undertaking a survey in connection with harbour improvements as the result of the seaway project having arrived at a further stage. I have in mind areas such as Sarnia where considerable work has been done by way of harbour improvement. I am not referring specifically to the item in the estimates for improvements this year. I assume it is anticipated that further improvements will be made in view of the completion of the St. Lawrence seaway.
There also seems to be an opinion that at the moment there is a bottleneck in the project in the form of the Welland canal. At the present time I believe it is capable of handling some 10 million tons a year, and I believe there are statements on record indicating that the tonnage will increase to 30 million. How soon that will be I do not know. From the point of view of making use of the seaway project to the fullest extent, I wonder whether it is going to be necessary to have another Welland canal side by side with the present one, so to speak, in order to take care of the increased tonnage. I would also like the minister to tell us if there are other bottlenecks that must be taken care of about which he can give us some information.

The vote before us now has nothing to do with lake levels. The lake level matter was disposed of by the international joint commission when the application by Ontario and New York state came before it. It dealt at full length with that question and recommended a method to protect lake levels on both shores of lake Ontario. That is why I stated earlier that

Supply-Transport
a control board has been established by the international joint commission for this purpose. I understand that the board is now dealing with the problem.
So far as the Chicago diversion is concerned, I made a statement in the house earlier on that matter. It is really one for the Secretary of State for External Affairs to deal with. It is an international matter arising out of the boundary waters treaty act and particularly out of a judgment of the supreme court of the United States. It is not covered in this vote, but I know it is a matter of keen concern to those of us who happen to live in the great lakes area. Canada has protested to the government of the United States against any further diversion, and where the matter is in congress I am unable to say.
Harbour improvements are not covered by this vote. Harbour improvements-
I was referring to surveys.

Surveys are not being made to improve harbours. They are only being made in connection with the international section of the seaway. In any event, it would be the Department of Public Works that would look into the question of harbour facilities. So far as the Welland canal is concerned, it provides for 25-foot navigation. As the hon. member knows, the over-all picture is a 27-foot channel which takes into account a further deepening at Welland of two feet. That is already provided in the over-all expenditure of $300 million which was voted by the house in 1951.

Can the minister give us
any fairly specific information as to what will happen to what is known as the Victoria bridge in Montreal with the advent of the seaway? Has any consideration been given to that matter, and what is likely to happen? Perhaps the final decision has not been made, but I should like that information before making any comment.

To answer that adequately would take some time, but let me do it as quickly as I can. In 1947 a board of engineers was established by the government to deal with the best method of developing the Lachine section, and in that study there is a reference to the bridges involved in the Lachine section. That report is a public report. It has been tabled in the house and can be seen. Unfortunately, however, it has been necessary to change some of the recommendations in the report because of the attitude of the Canadian National Railways and
[Mr. Chevrier.3
because of the greater cost of developing the Lachine section if the canal were on the north side rather than on the south side.
The plans have therefore been amended with a view, navigationwise only, of putting the canal in the Laprairie basin on the St. Lambert side. That will mean that studies will have to be undertaken of the bridges connecting the north and south shores. These studies are under way now, and it is with reference to these studies that consulting engineers have been engaged. The studies are not complete. All I can say is that I am hopeful from the preliminary reports I have received that there will be no undue delay in crossing these bridges because of the development.

It is very encouraging to hear the minister say that, because I think those of us in the city of Montreal who have thought about the matter at all are extremely perturbed. We know that this particular bottleneck, the Victoria bridge, is inadequate even at the present time to carry the traffic it is called upon to carry. We have heard rumours that a lift portion might be installed in the bridge in order to deal with canal traffic or that some other method might be adopted which would interrupt traffic on the bridge from time to time. Those of us who have crossed the bridge on Sunday night and have waited anywhere from fifteen minutes to an hour to make our way across because of the traffic jam realize that anything else that would interrupt traffic would be absolutely fatal. We are particularly perturbed because of the possibility of enemy action of some kind.
The bridge is practically a lifeline of the city, and we cannot think of evacuating the city on the one hand and on the other hand doing anything which would further obstruct traffic crossing the bridge. Therefore I am delighted to hear the minister say that every step will be taken to see that traffic over the bridge is not impeded. Perhaps in the course of these studies some way will be found to bring about a new bridge at that spot instead of the antique that is there at the present time. That would also be welcomed.

I should like to ask the minister how many labourers it is expected will be employed on this project in the year 1954. By that I do not mean engineers. There has been a great deal of talk about how much assistance is going to come to the unemployment problem by way of the St. Lawrence seaway project. How many workmen will be employed this year, 1954, and how many is it expected will be employed in 1955 and 1956?

That is really the $64 question. Let me answer it in this way. The surveys that were made by the economics branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce, which I used in 1951, indicated that when the work was at its peak some
15.000	workers would be employed.
That is by both Canada and the United States.

Yes. Recently I saw a statement by the Ontario hydro chairman that
10.000	workers would be employed when that work is at its peak. When my hon. friend asks how many will be employed in 1954, that will depend on how much progress can be made. In so far as the power end of it is concerned, there is nothing to stop commencement of the work immediately. I believe it will be possible next month to actually begin operations. As a matter of fact, the Ontario hydro now have a large number of workers in the international rapids section and so have we in the Department of Transport a number of workers in that section.
But ours are mostly engineers, are they not?

No, we have at least 110 men in the Lachine area, the Cornwall area and the Iroquois area. Some of these are working in co-operation with the Ontario hydro. How many more we employ in 1954 will depend on how soon we can determine whether we proceed alone or jointly with the province of Quebec, alone or jointly with the United States, and how soon Ontario begins the power work in the international rapids section, because we will have to follow not very far behind Ontario because of the fact the navigational work depends a great deal on the power development. I could only guess, and I would not like to guess. From that answer my hon. friend can see that it is somewhat difficult to reply to his question.

I realize that. I know it is difficult to say just how quickly this project is going to progress, how long it is going to take to reach its maximum point. As the minister indicated, we now have about 110 workmen on the power project. That is quite a few, but when you consider our tremendous unemployment problem, that number hardly enters the picture at all. Perhaps without going too far beyond the realms of possibility, the minister might indicate that during 1954, taking all the considerations into his calculations, he
Supply-Transport
may be able to give us an estimate that 500 or perhaps 1,000 might be employed. Perhaps I am away out, and it may be 10,000.
I believe the working people of Canada would like to know because so many people are already depending upon the work that is to be developed on this project. I understand that in Cornwall and Morrisburg the applications for employment have been growing and growing. In fact, people are going there in the expectation they are going to find employment because there has been so much talk about how much employment is going to be available when this St. Lawrence project gets under way. There is no better time that I know of than right now for the minister to make his statement which would be very enlightening to our unemployed.

I am afraid that it is difficult and I would not like to go too far out on a limb. I would not like to be held down by any figure. I have before me my deputy minister, who happened to be the superintendent when the Welland canal was constructed, and who has had quite a bit of experience, but he would hesitate to give any figure. He has indicated earlier that it will depend on the progress we can make. No one realizes more than I do the particularly difficult unemployment situation in the area from which I come. No one will be happier and more anxious to proceed as expeditiously as possible because of that situation. But whether there will be 2,000 employed in 1954, or more, I am unable to say. If it were possible to get the power works under way and a determination of the navigational features in the international section, I think it would be reasonable to expect that about
2,000	employees would be taken on.
That is in 1954.
Yes. Again I say this is a guess, and I am not competent to make a guess. I hope I will not be held too strictly to it.
With regard to the traffic between Montreal and the south shore, has any consideration been given to the possibility of building a tunnel between Montreal and the south shore?
Yes, it has, and the difficulties of a tunnel are such that we have decided against it.

I believe the minister has been sensible in not making a guess as to what the labour content in the St. Lawrence seaway is going to be. It is going to be a lot smaller than many people think. When the Canso

Supply-Transport
project was under consideration the estimate made at that time by engineers was that a labouring force of approximately 1,500 would be needed and it would take approximately three years to complete the job. The work will be finished a year ahead of time, and the labour content was 120. With the machinery that will be available in a few years' time, there will not be many pick and shovel men.
Press reports indicate that the areas around Cornwall and Prescott have been flooded with men looking for work; that is not necessary. I have been led to understand this work will go through the national employment offices, and if you are living in Vancouver or Sydney, Nova Scotia, you can determine the availability of work in any section through your own employment office without flooding one or two areas in Canada. I wish the minister would inform the house that the hiring for the project will be done through the national employment offices, and not by agents who have no responsibility to anyone.

I would certainly hope it would, otherwise there will be complete chaos. The national employment service office in an area is established for that specific purpose, and I presume the contractors and the hydroelectric commission as well as the seaway authorities, when they require men, will proceed to get them in that manner. That certainly would commend itself to me.

May I ask the minister whether there is any money to be voted in this year's estimates, either in the main estimates or in the supplementaries, for construction work on the seaway? Can he tell us roughly how the amount of work will be divided up between Ontario and the dominion? I presume a good many men will be employed by the Ontario hydro and not by the dominion at all.
Finally, could the minister explain further the situation with regard to the province of Quebec? He said in opening this discussion this morning that he had been in conference with the premier of Quebec. I am not clear as to just how that province fits into the picture. He mentioned not only power but also the seaway. My understanding is that Ontario is involved in so far as power was concerned, but not with the seaway, actually. I did not know that Quebec was involved, at all. However, that may be because of my own ignorance in the matter. If Quebec is involved, why did the minister wait until this very late date to negotiate with that province? It seems to me there should have been negotiations under way a long time ago, just as there have been with Ontario. An agreement was
[Mr. GUlis.l
reached with Ontario some years ago. I cannot understand why so recently the minister has gone down to talk this matter over with the premier of Quebec.

I shall be glad to answer these questions.
First, in conection with whether or not this vote contains anything for the actual construction of the St. Lawrence seaway. The answer is that it does not.
Is there any other vote?

Neither this vote nor any vote in the supplementary estimates, nor any other vote. They do not contain any allocation of money for the actual construction of the works on the seaway. That is provided for under the seaway authority which, I take it, will be established in due course by the government.
Then, with reference to the division as between Ontario and Quebec,-
Ontario and the dominion.

Ontario and the dominion, and also Quebec and the dominion. In the international rapids section there is a development of 2,200,000 horsepower. The agreement made with Ontario was that it would look after the power works and we would look after the navigation works. That has been cleared.
My hon. friend understands that, so far as the province of Quebec is concerned, there is at Lachine, just opposite the city of Montreal,
1,200,000	horsepower which could be developed, and to which the power engineers in 1947 addressed their recommendations. They found that it was possible for the federal government to build a channel 27 feet deep in the Lachine section to join with the other channel in the St. Francis, Soulanges, the international rapids and the Thousand Islands sections, up to the head of the lakes, as one alternative. They also found as another alternative the possibility of joint development of power and navigation; and that can be found in the report to which I referred earlier.
Then my hon. friend has asked: Why do you begin talking with the province of Quebec at this late date? Well, we have not started at this late date. Not very long after we entered into the agreement with Ontario, we started having talks with Quebec hydro. And it was with the assistance of Quebec hydro that it was possible to produce the report to which I referred earlier-a report which makes a recommendation for the joint development of power and navigation in the Lachine section, a report which was afterwards altered and the estimates changed because of rising costs, and the like.

Now, until quite recently the engineers of the Department of Transport and of the Quebec hydro were in consultation. They reached a point where they could not go any farther, and both agreed that talks should continue at a higher level. It was for that reason I proceeded to go down to Quebec city and to inquire from the premier of the province if the time had not arrived to give further consideration to these talks, and to refer the matter back again, with instructions from both governments, to see if it was not possible to arrive at some agreement. Whether it will be or not, I cannot say. And that really was the object of my visit.
This has nothing to do with the Americans?
No, not at all.
What sort of development does the dominion government favour? Does it want a joint seaway-power plan, or separate plans?
In the American section, do you mean?
No, so far as the Lachine section is concerned.

I do not think it makes any difference, so far as we are concerned. We can proceed either way. The only thing is this, that I think it would be better for the economy of the country to have a joint plan, because it stands to reason that if you are going to do power and navigation separately at two different times, it will cost more money than it would to do it jointly. And for that reason we thought that for the general benefit of the country as a whole it would be much better to develop them jointly. Of course it would mean a far greater expenditure. The total expenditure will be $400 million.
The total estimated cost?

Yes, as opposed to about $122 million for navigation alone.
Now, whether it is possible to make an agreement with Quebec in the same manner as we have made one with Ontario, I do not know. All I can say is that, from Ontario, there was the fullest possible co-operation; and I can say the same so far as my interview with the premier of Quebec is concerned. There was from him the fullest possible cooperation, and I am hopeful that it will be possible to develop that area jointly.

Referring to the number of persons directly employed, it has been my opinion that a far greater number of people will be employed in those industries supplying goods of one kind or another to be used in connection with this great project. What would be the ratio?
Well, that is a very difficult question to answer.

in part payment of that, together with the services of engineers in connection with the removal of the dam.

Mr. Chairman, I just wish to make a few remarks on this item. We realize that certain canals are important, particularly the Welland canal and others which are in use. The canals of this country were formerly very important, but there are many canals which, I believe, are becoming quite useless and, as has been indicated by the number of questions today, it seems to me we are spending a lot of money which may not be considered necessary.
With reference to the construction of canals, I think I would be rather remiss, coming from the maritimes, if I did not mention a canal for which we have asked consideration for quite a number of years and which today, I believe, is more important than it ever has been. I say that, Mr. Chairman, because of the proposed development of the St. Lawrence seaway. When that is developed I believe it will mean a great deal more coastal trade on the Atlantic coast with the United States and with South America. We are going to spend many millions of dollars for the development of the St. Lawrence seaway and that will be of great assistance to this country in trade with the United States as well as with overseas. The trade which is now being carried by trucks and railways from Canada to the United States and vice versa will, I believe, when the St. Lawrence seaway is constructed and on account of the cheapness of water transport, be all conveyed by our coastal steamers.
On the Atlantic coast, as we have pointed out time and time again, some 700 or 800 miles of route could be shortened by a canal across the Chignecto isthmus. We have asked little from this department or little from the government with reference to canals. I think the only canal we have in the maritime provinces is the St. Peters canal. From the estimates I noticed this morning that, of the

cost which the minister mentioned in connection with these canals, $47,000 has been spent for the St. Peters canal.
I am not recommending this project simply because I feel we in the maritime provinces should have more recognition, but because I believe that the Chignecto canal will be a real asset and that it is complementary to the development of the St. Lawrence seaway. I believe there is going to be a tremendous increase in this coastal trade. The development of this canal will save some 700 or 800 miles for this trade. As hon. members know, ships that have to go around Cape Breton and Nova Scotia run into the dangers of Sable island which I have understood has been called the graveyard of the Atlantic; it is a rather dangerous route. If a canal were constructed through the isthmus of Chignecto, you would have a sheltered route through the bay of Fundy and down the New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and American coast.
I should like to ask the minister if, in connection with the St. Lawrence seaway, any study has been made of this proposition as providing a shorter and more desirable route for trade with the United States and with South America? If no study or consideration has been given to it, I should like to ask whether his department would consider giving some study or consideration to this matter which I consider to be an extremely important one.

As the committee knows, this subject is one of keen interest to the members from the maritime provinces. I must say that no study has been given to the construction of the Chignecto canal in conjunction with the St. Lawrence seaway. The studies that were made having to do with the seaway were for the joint power and navigation development with the United States. The last studies that were made were carried out some years ago and, as my hon. friend knows, a report was tabled in the house; I have referred to it from time to time. I think the only way in which to give consideration to the construction of the Chignecto canal would be by the establishment of another such body. Whether the time is opportune for that action, I do not know; perhaps it is. I think that the house could not take any action-and certainly not by anything I could say at this time-unless a complete engineering study were made. It may be possible to do this at some time. I certainly would have no authority to say that it could not be done.

May I ask the minister this question? He can answer or not, just as he likes. Would he not consider it to be a
Supply-Transport
more practical proposition today than it has ever been considered to be in the past?
To that question I think I would have to answer yes.
I thank the minister.

Before this item passes I want to comment on the general way in which estimates are presented to us. What I have >to say applies to this particular item and in general to the presentation of estimates. Under "Canal services", we have six pages of estimates showing how many charwomen are employed in the system, how many messengers, how many typists, how many stenographers, how many gas engineers and electrical engineers and so forth. We have six pages devoted to giving us information as to the wage or salary paid to each one. The amount involved is something over $6 million. But when we get an item here of over $2 million, it is dismissed in two lines. All we have is "Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and new equipment". An item of over $2 million is dismissed in two lines in the estimates whereas six pages are taken to tell us how many typists, stenographers, charwomen and so forth are employed in the entire federal canal system.
I am simply suggesting that members of the committee would be much more interested in having more details about the acquisition and construction of the buildings, equipment and so forth than they are in knowing how many typists the system employs and what we pay those typists. That is a criticism that applies to the entire system of presenting estimates to the House of Commons.

I do not take it as a criticism, Mr. Chairman. I simply say to my hon. friend that the Department of Transport does not decide the manner in which estimates shall be tabled in the house. That is something that is done by the Department of Finance. That department determines the method. If the method is not a correct one, that is a matter for that department. I shall be glad to draw my hon. friend's remarks to the attention of the Minister of Finance. Perhaps when the estimates of the Department of Finance are before the committee, the hon. member as well might bring the matter to the attention of the minister.

I should like to say a word in support of the hon. member for Royal in his request concerning the Chignecto canal. I have not had the opportunity to make a thorough study of this canal but what I have learned greatly commends it to me. I believe that the governments have been

Supply-Transport
negligent concerning this matter. The mar-itimes certainly have the right to consideration of that sort, namely the building of a canal which would accomplish the saving mentioned by the hon. member. I think it is time that the minister set the necessary wheels in motion in order to have something done about this 'canal.

Mr. Chairman, I just came into the chamber a moment ago but I was greatly interested in hearing the remarks made by the minister with regard to the Chignecto canal and his statement that he thought the only proper way to consider the matter would be by the appointment of a royal commission. I had a good deal to do with the campaign a few years ago in connection with the Chignecto canal. I should like to say that I believe the people of the maritimes generally consider that that is exactly what should be done. We are not asking that the canal be built merely because it was a promise of confederation, although I think it undoubtedly was one. We believe that if a commission would inquire fully into the economic possibilities and benefits of that canal, it would bring in a favourable decision. What we should like to see is the appointment of a royal commission to make a comprehensive inquiry in the light of present-day conditions. Conditions have changed considerably, of course, since the days of the Surveyer commission, in 1931, I think it was. If a royal commission were appointed, I believe the people of the maritimes would be well satisfied to abide by its decision.

Item agreed to.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. When the committee rose at one o'clock I understand we were discussing item No. 448. Shall the item carry?

Item agreed to.
Marine service steamers-
449. Administration, operation and maintenance, $6,228,000.

I think this might be the place, if it is agreeable to the minister, to ask for a little information with respect to the fire boat in Montreal harbour. I notice that he has some 77 permanent firemen under this classification plus another 41 seasonal firemen, so I would think this is a good place

to ask the question. I also notice that he has three gentlemen who seem to have wandered over from the Department of Finance. They are called trimmers. He also has somebody who has probably come from the Secretary of State's department. It might even be the Secretary of State himself. He is called a boatswain's mate and gasman.
Coming directly to the fire boat itself, earlier in his estimates the minister pointed out that his department had entered into an arrangement with Vancouver by which they each share in the upkeep of a fire boat, and that nothing of the sort was being done at the present time in Montreal. I should like him to tell us first whether the situation with regard to the two ports is not somewhat different. It is my understanding that in Vancouver there is a good deal of city-owned property connected with the port and also a number of private docks, such as the C.P.R. dock, which have to be protected, whereas in Montreal the entire harbour is the property of the national harbours board. Perhaps we could get that out of the way as the first question.

Mr. Chairman, I had hoped that we could discuss this under the national harbours board estimates which are a little further on and which deal with this particular matter. They do not deal precisely with the matter in question but we certainly could discuss it under those items. I have no objection to discussing it now but if I do so I invite discussion on other items which is not clearly relevant. I wonder whether my hon. friend would allow it to stand until we get to the national harbours board items when I will deal with that point.
I will be very glad to. Would the minister like to give us a little bit of information as to what type of transportation and boats he is operating under this item and the type of work they are doing?

Yes, Mr. Chairman. This vote provides for the operation of all the steamers in the Department of Transport such as the d'Iberville, the new ship which was put into operation last year, the C. D. Howe, the Saurel and the Lady Laurier on the east coast, the Mackenzie and Estevan on the west coast, and a number of other ships in the Parry Sound district, the Prescott district, the Cornwall district and in the Montreal district. There are 32 such vessels being operated by the department under this vote.
Actually that was one of the things that interested me. I notice that there is provision for 30 masters, 19 permanent and 11 seasonal.
I did not hear that.
I notice that the minister has provided for 30 masters and apparently there are 32 boats in operation according to the statement he has made. On what basis are the other two operating?
I presume they are operating on an assistant basis. The officer who is before me tells me it is the practice to have a number of spares.
But already we have more boats than masters. We have 32 boats and 30 captains or masters, as the minister calls them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?
I am waiting for what is really an answer to a mathematical problem.
I will have to get the answer for my hon. friend. I do not have it available at the moment.
