speechtext: Shall the item carry?
I have no desire to hold up the item indefinitely but I would not like to see it go through because of the possibility of other questions arising from the answer to this one.
Could I not give my hon. friend the information during the consideration of these estimates?
Could we not let the item stand and proceed with the next one?

It has not been the practice to stand items. If we do that, I am afraid it will be difficult to make progress. I should like to get on with the estimates. I am sure my hon. friend will understand that with the number of votes in this department there is information that it is not always easy to obtain at a moment's notice, but I can assure him I will get the information for him.

I object strenuously to this procedure. I am asking what seems to me at least to be a perfectly reasonable question. I am told we have 32 boats in operation. I look at the estimates and I see that we have 30 masters. I therefore ask for an answer to the question. I am interested in that. I am told that the minister cannot immediately produce the answer, and that is all right, but then an attempt is made to say that I should go off in a corner and forget about the whole 83276-370
Supply-Transport
thing and the information will be given me later. But if I want to pursue any point that may arise out of the answer to the question then this item of the estimates will already have been disposed of.

Could I put it this way? The matter will not be closed. I will allow my hon. friend to bring it up on another relevant item. If there is not a relevant item then, as has been done before, it could be discussed on the last item of these estimates or the last item of the supplementary estimates. The information I have before me now is that there are 32 vessels which will be actively engaged in this service. I am not able to give the answer to the question at the moment, but I hope to be able to obtain it during the course of the day.
It is merely a matter of the minister getting the information from his officials.
That is right.

If that is the situation, why not let the item stand and come back to it as soon as the information has been obtained? As the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace has said, other questions may arise as the result of the answer the minister gives.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
I suggest that the minister will make progress if he lets the item stand and does not try to put it through without having given the information.

I was hopeful that the suggestion I made would be accepted. However, if it is not, I have no objection to the item standing.
Item stands.
Marine service steamers-
450. Construction or acquisition of vessels and equipment. $3,418,000.

In the details of this item I notice the heading "reconstruction and refit of stand-by vessel for Pacific ocean weather station 'P', $400,000." Would the minister tell us briefly what is the situation regarding Canada's contribution towards ocean weather stations? I realize that in some cases they are provided by the navy.

The position was this: By virtue of an agreement we are operating a weather station in the Atlantic, but that weather station has now been taken over by the United tates and we are operating a weather station in the Pacific. We have two ships which are used in the operation of that station. The expenditure, I am told, is to refit one as a stand-by.

Supply-Transport
What is the position now with regard to weather ships in the Pacific? I believe the United States did withdraw some of their ships. Has that difficulty been straightened out?

Yes. The United States gave notice, arising out of their representations to ICAO, that they intended to withdraw from the operation of weather stations, certainly those on the north Atlantic. There were objections from the member states of ICAO, and the result was it was decided to refer the whole matter to a conference in Paris at which the representatives of the various countries interested would be present. The conference took place, with the result that the position is somewhat altered, but in the main the principle is the same, namely that practically all the weather ships in the Atlantic and those in the Pacific remain, with the exception of one ship which will be taken over by other member states. It may be-I am not too sure about this-that one of the stations has disappeared. But in any event, this particular station remains as it was.
Why did the United States take that stand? It never seemed to make sense to me that they would withdraw this weather ship.

I believe it was a question of cost. If my hon. friend recalls, there was a great deal of discussion in congress about the tremendous costs, not so much of weather ships, but of defence installations generally. I presume that one of the items that was looked at towards the reduction of that cost was weather ships. With new equipment and so forth, it becomes perhaps a little easier to fly across the Atlantic than it was in the earlier days. However, Canada feels that the weather ships are of great importance to the safety of aircraft, and feels they should not be removed. We have maintained that position. I believe one of the main reasons was one of cost.

Item agreed to.
Aids to navigation-
452. Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and new equipment, $1,586,720.

This item covers the construction and acquisition of equipment for navigational aids. The minister may possibly recall that during the session of 1951 I raised with him the question of the extension of navigational aids in the bay of Fundy. The minister did not have the information available at that time but he promised me he would communicate with me afterwards. With the courtesy which I have usually experienced

from him, we exchanged correspondence during the summer dealing with this matter. The result was that the minister said he felt that it was impossible at that time to provide additional navigational aids in the bay of Fundy because of the amount of money involved, but he would keep it under consideration and when funds were available he would hope to deal with this matter.
It may be, Mr. Chairman, that in this additional vote we have here today, the minister has provided for that. I have not had the opportunity of discussing this with him. As he knows, I have been out of the house for various reasons and have not had the opportunity of discussing the matter with him personally. As I pointed out to him at that time, from Digby at Point Prim to Spencer's island, a distance of roughly 100 miles, there are no aids to navigation whatever except the ones listed by the minister in the correspondence he sent me. If the minister has that list in front of him, he will find that in every case they are fixed lights and not whistling buoys or horns or anything of that description.
Although the minister did point out that I had raised specifically the matter of Halls Harbour, there were only a few boats operating out of that port. However, there are many other boats operating in the bay of Fundy. There are the gypsum boats and the pulp and paper boats, carrying cargo and people. While we have lighthouses, the minister told us about his experience of flying over the vast expanses of the Atlantic and seeing the conditions under which lighthouses operate. I suggest that if he were out on the bay of Fundy on a foggy day with a heavy surf running, he would find the fixed light would be of very little assistance. The requirement is for sound buoys of some kind, something on which you can get a bearing. Now, you go up the most dangerous waters in the world, with the highest tide and the heaviest currents, and you have a 90-mile expanse from Digby at Point Prim to Spencer's island without a single buoy or foghorn on which you can get a bearing. This is a serious situation.
The minister suggested it would cost perhaps $5,000 to put in a whistling buoy. Costs may have gone up since 1951, but I doubt if they have gone up very much. We have ^ yote here of $127 million for this department. I suggest the time has come when, if the minister has not decided to do something about it, he should do so now. He very modestly disclaimed any desire to have the Canso causeway named the Chevrier causeway. We have heard rumours that possibly the minister will retire from this department. I hope that is not true. I can assure

him of this. If he will accept my request I will see that any buoy that is placed out in the bay of Fundy is called the Chevrier buoy, and the minister will have the everlasting gratitude of the fishermen.

Perhaps we could call it the Chevrier girl, after one of my daughters. On more than one occasion the hon. member has brought this matter to my attention, and as he says there has been some correspondence in connection with it. There are a number of works provided for in the bay of Fundy, but unfortunately we have not yet been able to provide for the particular project mentioned by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings. One of my officers here nods his head, and whether that means that he is going to do it or not-

Can you get him to nod it
more affirmatively?
-I know that at least it will be given consideration for the next fiscal year.

I notice this item concerns aids to navigation and I am wondering whether I would be in order in raising a question that pertains to obstructions to navigation? While we are considering this item, will the minister make a statement as to the situation in respect to the removal of Ripple rock? What are the results of the experimental borings which were undertaken some time ago?

I can get the house this information, that this matter has now been referred to another department. Ripple rock is no longer a matter to be determined by the estimates of the Department of Transport. I do not think it ever was. It was always under the Department of Public Works. But a special committee has been given instructions, in conjunction with the national research council, to deal with this matter, and the responsibility for it has been assigned, I believe either to the Minister of Public Works or to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I am not sure which. But it no longer comes under this department.

At page 525, in the explanatory notes, I notice an amount for the removal of obstructions in navigable waters. The estimate is increased from $32,000 to $100,000. Would the minister explain this large increase?
That is for lake Erie, and it is due to the removal of a number of wrecks lying adjacent to the lake channel.

Item agreed to.
83276-370i
Supply-Transport Nautical services-
453. Administration, operation and maintenance, including grants and contributions for the purposes indicated in the details of the estimates; rewards for saving life from vessels in distress; subsidies to salvage companies, and the payment of expenses, including excepted expenses, incurred in respect of Canadian distressed seamen as defined in section 306 of the Canada Shipping Act, $474,764.

Mr. Chairman, there are two questions I should like to ask. This item, I see, deals with the operation and maintenance of nautical services. My first question has to do with the establishment of a coastguard service. The hon. member for Nanaimo dealt with this matter at some length on an earlier occasion when the estimates of this department were under consideration. I do not want to add anything to what he said, but I would like to ask the minister if he would take the lead in having another investigation made of this question.
For some years now we have had the search and rescue service and, while it has done good work, it is becoming increasingly clear that such service is not going to be sufficient for very long. I believe steps would now be taken by the government to have a further investigation made. About six weeks ago the tugboat men on the west coast formed their own rescue team, because they felt that the service available was not satisfactory.
I have here a dispatch from the Vancouver Sun of April 23 bearing the heading "Tug-boaters Form Own Rescue Team". It continues with the subheading "Ottawa Refusal of Coastguard Angers Industry", and the first paragraph is as follows:
British Columbia towboat men, fed up with Ottawa's cool attitude to demands for formation of a coastguard, today completed plans for a tugboat rescue unit which will attempt to fill the gap.
There should not be an obligation on the men in the industries to take steps of that kind. Of necessity such arrangements will not be as thorough or as efficient as if there were a proper coastguard service. Time and again we have accidents on the west coast. United States coastguard vessels are there to render help. I know that sometimes the Canadian vessels help the Americans. There is very close co-operation between the ships of the two nations.
However, I suggest that the development of the west coast has now reached a stage where there should be established a proper coastguard service. We have now the big aluminum plant at Kitimat. A city is being established there which, eventually, will be of about 30,000 people. The whole of the coast is opening up, and there is far more traffic on those waters than there has been before. As the minister knows the waters are extremely dangerous.

Supply-Transport
I believe the situation is summed up very well in an editorial which appeared eight days ago in the Vancouver Sun. This editorial, dated June 3, is headed "Coastguard Still Needed". The editorial states-and I shall read only two paragraphs-
Logic is not the Liberal government's strongest point.
The Sun, of course, is an ardent supporter of this government, and the leading newspaper supporter in the west.
And a very ardent admirer of mine, too, I notice.

Yes, sometimes. The editorial continues:
It has again turned down a request for a Canadian coastguard saying there's no need, because R.C.A.F. and marine agencies co-operate quite happily to rescue ships in distress.
This is, obviously, proof that a regularly established, fully manned, highly trained Canadian coastguard with correctly designed ships-
Of course that is another very important feature.
-would be even more successful than a semiofficial and voluntary rescue service. But the government can't or won't see all the benefits from a separate coastguard service.
On this Pacific coast air force and tug companies have allied to set up a rescue team. They've done good work. On this basis alone the worth of a proper service has been proved.
Would the minister comment on the suggestion that the government departments should have another look at this question as to whether or not the time has come to establish a proper coastguard service? I have another question under this item, but it does not refer to this service.

As my hon. friend knows, and as I indicated earlier, the matter of protection of coasts was referred to an interdepartmental committee some years ago. As I also indicated, the chairman of that committee was a distinguished jurist of the province of British Columbia who, at the time, was chairman of the maritime commission.
The result of the investigation was a recommendation to place under the air rescue division of the Department of National Defence the protection of our coasts in the manner set out in that report. It may be that the time has arrived to take another look; I am not prepared to say that it has not. But I am sure it is a matter that my hon. friend would realize would be very costly. If it was estimated to cost $9 million or $10 million then, it would probably cost far more than that today.
However, it may be that other means can be found. As my hon. friend knows, the

matter is not under the Department of Transport any longer. It is handled by a division of the Department of National Defence.
Exclusively?

Oh yes-search and rescue. However, I shall be glad to bring it to the attention of my colleague the Minister of National Defence to see if, because of present conditions, it is not advisable to ask the interdepartmental committee which dealt with the matter in 1951 to take another look at the situation today, in view of changed circumstances.
Was it the recommendation of that committee that this system of having the air force in charge of the air rescue service would be permanent; or was it merely a temporary arrangement?

I do not think it was either permanent or temporary. I think it was one of the recommendations that came out of this investigation, and we simply adopted it. There is nothing permanent about any of these arrangements; but if it works well I think perhaps it should be permanent. On the other hand, if it does not work well there is no reason why it should not be changed.

I wonder if the minister would clear up a point for me in this connection. I was not quite sure the other day, when he and I had an exchange in connection with this matter, whether the $9 million or $10 million to which he referred at that time, and to which he has referred again this afternoon, was to cover the cost of the coastguard on the Pacific coast, or the cost of the coastguard service on the Atlantic coast, the Pacific coast and the great lakes- the whole of them.
Yes; the total cost of the $9 million covers the east and west coasts and also the great lakes.
I think the minister said the estimated cost of operation was between $3 million and $3,500,000.
Yes; the capital cost was $9,033,000 and the operational and maintenance costs $3,284,000. This was in 1950. I was in error a moment ago; it was one year earlier.
Was that estimate broken down into three areas, Pacific, Atlantic and the great lakes?
It was by the committee; the figures I have are general figures.
Can the minister give us the figures of cost for the west coast?

As I say, I have not the figures; they were not given to me. I presume they were broken down for the committee, but I have never received any report as to a break-down. If they are available I will ask the present chairman of the maritime commission to give them to my hon. friend.

In view of the fact that the minister has said that there is a possibility of some new inquiry being made into the situation with respect to coastal protection for British Columbia, I feel I should suggest to him that there should be included in it some analysis of the actual situation with respect to the existing lifeboat stations on the west coast of Vancouver island. Representations have been made to me which indicate that in point of fact, under conditions as they exist at the present time, the expenditure on these lifeboat stations is not one which is resulting in the best services that can be obtained for an expenditure of that kind of money. I am not attempting to make any dogmatic statement on this point, but it has been suggested to me that within the limitations that are imposed upon them by the type of equipment and so on that is provided, a good job is being done. But nevertheless many situations arise on the west coast of Vancouver island at the present time, owing to larger fishing boats going farther and farther to sea, that indicate that the set-up as we have it at the present time is not really the most effective one that we could have. I would suggest that if this matter is to be looked into that question should also be included in the terms of reference, or whatever one might call what is to be investigated.
I should think that if investigations were made-and I am not saying they will be-they should cover the whole field.

I have one other question to raise on this item. It has to do with vocational training for merchant seamen. In the details which we find on page 527 is included an item of $3,000 for the training of merchant seamen. As the minister knows, a great many Canadian merchant seamen have been forced onto the beach in the last few months because of the transfer of Canadian ships to United Kingdom registry. The very least that this country could do would be to give these men every facility to train for another occupation. Some of them have been merchant seamen for quite a long time. Many of them served during the war, and have served for ten years or fifteen years. It is not very pleasant
Supply-Transport
to be forced out of your occupation after that length of time and have to try to find new work.
I do not understand why the government is reducing this vote. Last year it was $9,000. This year it is only $3,000. We were told in the veterans affairs committee a few days ago that a recommendation had been submitted to the government for the setting up of an adequate vocational training plan for those merchant seamen. Apparently that had been considered by the Department of Transport, the Department of Labour and possibly the Department of Veterans Affairs. I am not sure whether that last department is involved but, in any event, from the departments of labour and transport there was a submission for the establishment of a proper vocational training scheme which would have helped those several hundred seamen who had been displaced because the government has allowed Canadian ships to be transferred to United Kingdom registry, with the result that the ships have to carry a United Kingdom crew. I wish the minister would explain why it was the government rejected that proposal, and I hope it is not yet too late for provision to be made to give those men adequate vocational training.

I must say that I am not aware of any scheme that was rejected by the government that provided for vocational training for merchant seamen. Certainly, none has come to my attention. Certainly, no representations have been made to my department. The only thing I have any knowledge of is vocational training under the federal-provincial agreements. By virtue of the agreement which the federal government, through the Department of Labour, makes with provincial governments, there is I understand some provision for training various groups of people for a calling. My understanding is that the attention of the Minister of Labour has been drawn to this matter and that he has taken it up with the provinces. He has been in communication with the provinces about it, but beyond that I can add nothing other than to say that no representations have been made to me as Minister of Transport.

We had a pretty definite statement, I think it was from an official of the Department of Labour, and Captain Slocombe of the minister's department was there. I think he confirmed it, or he could have been the one who made the original statement; but in any event, it was made perfectly clear that plans had been made for setting up vocational training for those men who have

Supply-Transport
been displaced because the Canadian vessels are now being operated under the British flag. Frankly, I do not see why such a training scheme should not be set up. It does seem very unfair to these men just to force them on the beach.
The minister has suggested that they could get the regular vocational training. We cross-examined on that point also in the committee on veterans affairs. It was pointed out that to put these men under the ordinary vocational training would mean this: in the first place that some of the provinces have not agreed to that; some of them are not parties to the training scheme. One of the provinces, my own province of British Columbia, does not pay any allowances, apparently, while the men are taking vocational training. If they had the benefits of the scheme which was worked out between the provinces and the departments of transport, veterans affairs and labour in 1948 or 1949, the men would be eligible for allowances and they would have much wider benefits than they could get simply as ordinary unemployed men. Will the minister look into that situation to see whether or not some provision can be made to give these men opportunities for taking training?

Mr. Chairman, I may be mistaken but I have to repeat that I have no personal recollection of any scheme such as that which my hon. friend has in mind. I think what the hon. member is driving at is a scheme which the Department of Labour had in mind with reference to the training of these merchant seamen following the decision of the government to transfer certain ships to the United Kingdom, and I think that scheme was a purely provincial-federal one which is to be handled by the Minister of Labour. However, I will be glad to bring that to his attention because the part of the vote which deals with vocational training is not one which would cover a scheme such as my hon. friend has in mind, and I am quite sure he will readily realize that. In any event I will bring what he has said to the attention of the Minister of Labour to ascertain whether it is possible to give the assistance such as he has mentioned.

Item agreed to.
Pilotage service-
455. Administration, operation and maintenance, including authority for temporary recoverable advances not exceeding $20,000, $540,983.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to give an example of real pilotage. A young couple from Fort William had their tickets for England and while going through the United States someone stole their grips, and
'Mr. Green.]
their tickets were of course lost. I placed the matter before the minister and within ten minutes he assured them they would be on their way the next day, and they were on their way the next day to England. This may be out of order, Mr. Chairman, but it is a credit to the minister and shows he is efficient and has a heart.

Item agreed to.
457. Steamship inspection, including the carrying out of the provisions of the conventions for the safety of life at sea and load lines, and a contribution of $7,000 to the province of Nova Scotia, department of education, $646,853.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister would comment on this item, for I notice there is an increase of $67,000. I doubt if this can be attributable to the introduction of the five-day week, because these are largely technical personnel. Is this an increase in the staff of the minister's department, or is there some other explanation?
It represents exclusively the increase in salary which came into effect in December of last year.

Could the minister also give an explanation for the $7,000 grant to the Nova Scotia department of education? I have discussed this matter with the minister before and he is aware of my views. I realize the statute will have to be carried out but I think, Mr. Chairman, there has been perhaps a great deal of misunderstanding. Certainly there has been considerable complaint on the part of those engaged in coastwise shipping along the Atlantic coast as regards the incidence of this inspection service. The steamships engaged in coastal shipping feel they are placed at a great disadvantage by having to comply with the stringent regulations which are enforced by this department, particularly when competitors are not required to do so. I hope that the increase in staff is not brought about by increased inspection of small fishing boats around the coast, because although the minister has been most helpful in alleviating instances of too stringent application of these regulations I think they are causing a great deal of trouble and, I would say quite frankly, incurring unnecessary expense. I hope and believe that as long as the minister is here he will see that this administration is kept to a minimum, and I hope it will be restricted still further. The increase is not excessive but I think it could be dispensed with altogether.
We cannot-
What about the $7,000?

That is a contribution to Halifax for the marine school to assist in the training of engineers and improving the facilities and standards of instruction in the province's marine engineering school in order to prepare candidates for the Department of Transport examination in marine engineering.

Mr. Chairman, this covers the steamship inspection service. About two months ago there was a deep sea tug called the Chelan lost on the west coast with 14 lives, and it appears that in the inquiry which was held it was found there had been some new steering gear installed in this vessel which had not been inspected by government inspectors. I took it from the report that the government inspectors complained that the ship's owner or master was responsible for not seeing that that inspection was carried out. Apparently the government inspectors had been shown plans of this new steering gear, but it was never inspected at sea and, as I said, the ship was lost with all hands. This sort of thing should not happen. I do not know whether there was any fault on the part of the government. There might have been. I would like to know what provisions are made for the inspection of a vessel under these conditions. These boats should not be allowed to go to sea when there have been changes made of that type without adequate inspection. It may be the regulations are not sufficient to cover a situation of that kind, but I would ask the minister to explain what happened in this particular case.

Mr. Chairman, of course I am not familiar with this particular case. Many casualties occur in Canada and it would be difficult to deal with them all, but I remember some publicity in the press in connection with the Chelan and I know generally what the steamship inspection regulations call for. There are steamship inspectors all across Canada. There are quite a number of them in Vancouver, some in Victoria, and some in Prince Rupert, and it is the responsibility of those inspectors to inspect vessels from time to time. I am informed that it is a yearly inspection, and I am told now that when the inspector comes around and finds something faulty he serves notice on the master and the master is required to take care of the faulty equipment.
I am informed that in the case of the Chelan the steering gear was known to be of a good type. With reference to the casualties I might say that casualties do take place on the coasts, on the St. Lawrence, and on the great lakes, not because of lack of inspection
Supply-Transport
but because of weather conditions, and also because of faulty equipment of which we are not aware.
I think the steamship inspection department tries to advise and does advise its inspectors to make a regular inspection of these vessels. I might add that there are casualties not only at sea, but in the air and on the ground, which are not the fault of the Department of Transport officials. For instance, as regards the Chelan, I believe there was a terrific storm, and certainly under those conditions it becomes difficult for any vessel, no matter if properly equipped, to withstand the elements. It might have been because the captain did not know the storm was coming up; it might have been because the radio was not in operation; and it might well have been that in taking a chance he found himself in difficulties from which he could not extricate himself.

Is there any obligation on the company to have new steering gear inspected before sending the vessel to sea? The minister has dealt with the annual inspection, but that is another matter. This disaster had nothing to do with the annual inspection. It presumably was caused by defective steering gear which had just been installed. One of the newspaper dispatches has this comment:
James Moorcroft, a government steamship inspector, informed the deputy coroner, Dr. A. G. Grim-son, that it was the duty of the company officials to inform his office when a ship was ready for sea after undergoing important repairs.
He told the court that his department had not inspected the vessel between the time she had changes made to her steering apparatus and the time she went on her last and fatal cruise.
That is a report of the statement made by the minister's inspector. Mr. Moorcroft may be the chief inspector, although I am not sure. Another dispatch with regard to the same inquest states:
New hydraulic steering gear installed in the Vancouver tug Chelan shortly before her last, fatal voyage had not been tested at sea by government steamship inspectors.
This was revealed Friday in testimony at the inquest in Vancouver into the death of Frank Hykaway, one of the fourteen victims of the Chelan shipwreck in Alaskan waters April 15.
Canadian government steamship inspector James Moorcroft said plans for installation of the new steering gear might have been submitted to his office without his knowledge.
But, he said, after such a change in the vessel's equipment, a steamship inspector should have been taken along when the gear was tested.
It would look as though the owners had been extremely negligent in not having an inspection made. I am not blaming the government inspector because I do not think he was at fault. However, either the owners failed to comply with the regulations or there

Supply-Transport
is no regulation which compels them to have the vessel inspected in a case such as this. Can the minister tell us which of those situations actually exists?

If I may say so, I do not think it is either. I am informed that the company installed new hydraulic steering gear without advising the inspector and without advising the department. After the preliminary investigation which was made by our people, it did not appear that the steering gear could have been the cause of the casualty.

Item agreed to.
River St. Lawrence ship channel service-
460. Contract dredging, $2,500,000.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the minister and the committee will not mind coming inland to the great lakes for a short period and to get away from salt water for a while. I notice that the total estimates of the department amount to $127 million approximately and that this item for contract dredging is $2,500,000. I am just wondering whether that money is all well spent. What makes me a little bit curious about the matter is this. At Kincardine on lake Huron we have a harbour at the mouth of a river. Each year, as a rule, that harbour has to be dredged. I would suggest that if the department had a better liaison with the public works department, they would eventually come to the conclusion that they would save money by building a proper harbour in a location like that, thereby getting away from this foolish spending of money which has been going on for a great number of years in connection with the harbour at Kincardine.
In connection with the Kincardine harbour I may say that in the public works department there are plans that have been there for a number of years for the building of a proper harbour but the department never got around to doing it. I leave that suggestion with the minister, namely that he talk the matter over with the Department of Public Works and see whether they could not save money by doing away with unnecessary dredging in Kincardine harbour every year.

The minister may recall that earlier in the year I raised the question of dredging in the eastern gap or eastern channel, as it is called, in Toronto harbour, and that he was good enough to put the machinery in motion to have that dredging done. The point was that the channel silts up in the winter. We in Toronto were looking forward to the resumption of the operation of the steamship Cayuga, which has been put into service again by Toronto people. It has a fourteen-foot draft and we wanted to be sure

that in June, when service was resumed, it would pass readily through the channel.
I am not sure what happened but I want to take this opportunity to inquire. I understood that the minister at the time put the matter in motion but that there was some delay in connection with tenders. Actually we find that tenders were recalled again later and I believe the dredging has not yet been done. I should like to know ju,;t what happened and what the situation is. At the same time perhaps the minister would indicate-if this is the item under which provision is made for dredging in the Toronto area; and I am not sure that it is-what amount is estimated to be spent this year for dredging in Toronto harbour and who are the contractors.

Mr. Chairman, unfortunately I find myself unable to answer my hon. friend's question for this reason. The administration of the Toronto harbour is under the jurisdiction of the Toronto harbour commission. While it is true that they report to me for amendments to their statute from time to time they are, by their statute, authorized to administer all matters in connection with the harbour. However, from time to time they seek to have dredging work done, but that dredging is done by the Department of Public Works. Hence I am unfortunately not able to answer my hon. friend's question.
Item agreed to.

The hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace asked why there were 32 boats and only 30 masters.
