That is the information that has been given to me.
That is, there are two small vessels additional to the 32 the minister listed previously?
No.
That is what the minister said.
So I am told.
So we have 30 regular vessels with masters and two small ones that do not require master's certificates. Is that right?
So I am told.
Thank you.

On item 449, may I point out that in the particulars at page 521 will be found an item of $25,000 for the charter of aircraft for aerial ice survey. Can the minister tell us whether or not that work is done by private firms?
Yes. It is done by private contract which is awarded by the air transport board. It is the ice patrol work in the spring.
That work is not done by the R.C.A.F?
No; it is not.

Then immediately below the one I have just mentioned there is a further item of $120,000. It is a new item apparently. It is described as "Charter of vessels for northern transportation". What is meant by that? Does the government charter vessels in addition to having its own? What vessels are covered by that vote?

Yes. In connection with the trips of the d'Iberville and the C. D. Howe to northern Canada, particularly the d'Iberville, as my hon. friend knows the latter ship will take in this year the supplies for all our weather stations in the Queen Elizabeth islands with the exception of the most northerly one, Alert Bay, and we hope to take in the supplies for Alert Bay in 1955. In order to supply these stations it is necessary over and above the d'Iberville to have one dry cargo and one tanker vessel. The three ships form a sort of convoy. The two additional ships are chartered, and this is the amount of money required for their services.

Is this the first year that has
been done?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Railway and steamship services-
462. Repairs and expenses in connection with the operation and maintenance of official railway cars under the jurisdiction of the department. $56,240.
S upp ly-Transport

This is the first item of the
railway services. I should like to ask the minister a question with regard to the Pacific Great Eastern Railway. Last week the premier of British Columbia made a statement to the effect that he had presented to Ottawa a request for assistance in the extension of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway to the Peace river district from Prince George and from Squamish to North Vancouver. The newspaper report reads as follows:
Premier Bennett feels confident the federal government will share the $60 million estimated cost of building the southern and northern extensions of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway. "I expect the federal government will pay 50 per cent of the cost", Bennett said in Victoria Tuesday when he announced that tenders for a railway bridge across the Capilano river in West Vancouver will be called next week.
Will the minister explain whether or not the premier of British Columbia is correct in his statement and what the policy of the government is with respect to assistance for these extensions? I would remind the minister that only a few years ago he brought in a bill which provided a subsidy for the extension of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway from Quesnel to Prince George. I have Hansard here for the second session of 1949 containing the minister's remarks at that time. As found at page 1443, he had this to say:
The construction of this extension will provide traffic for the railway and assist in developing the natural resources in the area consisting of large tracts of timber suitable for lumber, newsprint, pulpwood and plywood, mining possibilities, sections of agricultural and grazing lands, hydroelectric power potentialities, and sport and recreational attractions.
He went on to justify the granting of the subsidy, which was set at $15,000 a mile. It was not as heavy as the subsidy for which the present premier is asking. The present Minister of Fisheries also spoke in that debate and he made some very sound remarks which are still applicable today. Here is what he said, as found on page 1450:
I want to warn hon. members, however, that when this subsidy of $15,000 a mile for this construction is passed I do not think it will be the last time this house will be asked to help in the extension of the P.G.E.
Of course the Minister of Fisheries has now proved to be right about that.
Premier Johnson's-
He was the coalition premier, and not a Social Credit premier.
-avowed purpose in connection with that railway is to do what was originally intended; that is, push it through the Rocky mountains into the Peace river block, where there is great traffic in wheat and in the finest anthracite coal in Canada, and where there are also potential oil fields.

Supply-Transport
Of course that was before the Minister of Fisheries was in the cabinet. He also had this to say:
I want to just mention this briefly, because when we are passing this appropriation I think we should be fully aware of all the implications, since we are committing ourselves to a policy of subsidizing the extension of this provincial railway.
The last paragraph of his speech reads as follows:
This investment which we are now making in the P.G.E. has long been needed. I believe it will be well worth while. Premier Johnson is to be congratulated on being the provincial premier who, at last, is doing something positive about the P.G.E.
Of course Premier Bennett is now proposing to do far more about the P.G.E. than Premier Johnson ever did.
I think this federal government is to be congratulated also on helping him in this effort to expand the P.G.E.
What I want to know from the minister is whether or not he is going to help in this planned extension. He has dealt with the Pacific Great Eastern Railway twice in the house within the last few weeks. When we were discussing the extension of the C.N.R. into the Chibougamau area the Minister of Transport had this to say, as found at page 4599 of Hansard of May 11:
Some subsidy on such a line may well be justified as it was in the case of the northward extension of the Pacific Great Eastern in 1949 . . .
Again, on May 19 the minister made another statement. I will read from the English translation. I could not follow him when he was speaking but I checked the translation afterwards and I find that this is what he had to say:
The government's policy is to encourage lines which can operate at a profit. These two lines were provincial. The first of these two railways belongs to the British Columbia government and this government wished to extend its trackage. To this end they requested a subsidy, which was granted them.
Here we are with this question on our doorstep. The premier of British Columbia submitted a brief last fall outlining in detail the merits of the extension of this railway. I do not need to go into that any further. What I should like to know is whether the dominion government is prepared to subsidize these extensions. If not, why has it changed its policy since 1949 when it was so strongly in favour of subsidizing the extension of this same railway?

I do not want to disappoint my hon. friend, but I am sure he wants to be fair. We are now dealing with a particular item of the railway estimates, and he has introduced a subject which could certainly last for hours, because I see there are other

hon. members who would like to discuss it. We had an opportunity when the Chibougamau railway extension-
No.

Oh yes. There was an
opportunity to discuss this matter and it was discussed then. Inasmuch as I do not want to be disrespectful to my hon. friend I will deal with the matter but I do hope that he and other hon. members who are interested in it will not take this opportunity to debate it at length because I do not think this is the place to do it. The hon. member refers to a statement made by the premier of British Columbia. I cannot comment on that statement except to say that the government has received an application from the premier of British Columbia for a subsidy on the P.G.E. from Squamish to Vancouver. In fact, the application is a pretty lengthy one and goes into the economics of the Pacific Great Eastern at some length. I think it is safe to say that legislation has already been passed in the British Columbia legislature providing for financial assistance towards the construction of certain railway lines.
I believe it is the intention of the British Columbia government to give consideration to two matters, first, the extension from Squamish to Vancouver, and second, the extension from Prince George to the Peace river block by way of Hudson Hope on to Hines Creek or Dawson Creek. I am not too sure which it is, but in any event it is in that general northeasterly direction, and the purpose is to provide a link with the Northern Alberta railway. The application which has come to the government deals specifically with the southern end of the line only, namely, the extension from Squamish to Vancouver. This application will have to be given careful consideration. Now, when my hon. friend asks what is the policy of the government, the stock answer is that it will be announced in due course. In this case it cannot be stated until consideration has been given to this application.
When the Canadian National Railways desire to build a line, we give it very careful consideration. First, the Canadian National gives it study, and then we consider it in order to satisfy ourselves that it is advisable. I do not know enough about the extension in question. All I know is that we did give a subsidy to extend the line from Quesnel to Prince George because we were convinced that was the right thing to do. Until a study has been made of this southern extension, and that is all I think that is before us at the moment, it would not be proper for me to

give any further indication. I presume that in due course the matter will be given careful study, and following that an announcement will be made.

On that point, the railway was up in the air at both ends until the connection was made from Quesnel to Prince George, where it connected with the Canadian National line. At the southern end there is this gap between Squamish and North Vancouver. The government admitted the justice of asking for a subsidy for the northern extension. Now, what justification could there be for refusing to give a subsidy to finish the line at the other end?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am afraid it was my own unfamiliarity with the subject matter of item 462 that caused me to allow the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra to proceed as far with his remarks as he did. Having done so, I felt that I should allow the minister to reply. I feel I should point out now that this item has to do with the operation and maintenance of official railway cars. I do not see how, in the light of that, I could justify a discussion on the Pacific Great Eastern Railway.

Since the question has been asked about policy, I assure the minister it is not my intention at this stage or perhaps any other stage at this session to debate the question of the extension of the railway into the northern Alberta area, but I would appreciate it if the minister could say whether his department has formulated any policy with respect to the assistance of such railways, other than the procedures that have been laid down in such extensions as the one from Quesnel to Prince George. If he could just clarify that matter at the moment, It would be a great help.

All I can say, Mr. Chairman, is that it has been our general policy, when dealing with Canadian National extensions, to look at the profitability or non-profitability of the line. Unless the Canadian National Railways were able to convince us and we were able to convince ourselves that it was a profitable thing to construct the line, then we would not do it. In a number of cases, at least four if not five since I have been in the department, we have been convinced of the economics of such lines. We have brought bills before the house to build such lines.
There have been exceptions to that policy, and it was an exception when we granted the subsidy to the Pacific Great Eastern to build from Quesnel to Prince George. I believe that was an exception that was well justified because it was a provincial railway 83276-371J
Supply-Transport
that began nowhere and ended nowhere, and I say that respectfully. We felt it should end at least on the main line of the Canadian National Railways at Prince George, so I feel that extension was a reasonable action. Now, whether or not it will be a reasonable thing to extend it southward or even northward into the Peace river district is a matter that requires study. I am sure the house would not want me to prejudge the application that has been made by the government of British Columbia at this stage, when no study has been given. I believe we will study it carefully, and I am sure as sympathetically as we have studied the other, because I know that that whole Pacific area requires an outlet. Whether the outlet should be as suggested in the application or in some other form, I am not able to say, but there should unquestionably be an outlet. I think perhaps it should be envisaged with that in view.
I thank the minister.

My remarks perhaps should have been made on a previous item, but I will be in order by confining my remarks to this item. Representations have been made to me protesting against the proposal to make liquor available on railway trains. I understand that the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific have made representations with that in view, and I am sure the minister will be concerned that this should not be made available in the official cars. It has been represented to me that we really do not require any increase in the number or variety of outlets for liquor, and also if liquor is offered for sale on the trains which are common carriers it will present a problem to the minors of the country. There is a question as to whether municipalities through which these trains will be operating should not be permitted to vote on the question before any permission is given. I wonder if the minister could indicate what the cabinet policy is on this question?

I quite realize why my hon. friend would be interested in this particular problem. While I have an opinion on the problem, and I am sure each member of the cabinet has, it is one which does not concern us. The sale of liquor is governed by the laws of the province. As my hon. friend knows, there are some provinces that prohibit the sale of liquor, whereas there are others which do not, so I am informed, certainly in the manner which my hon. friend has in mind. In any event, I could not speak with any degree of authority for the Canadian Pacific Railway. They determine their own policy as to whether or not they will

Supply-Transport
sell liquor on their trains, in accordance with the laws of the province through which the train proceeds. The same applies to the Canadian National Railways, save and except this, that I can bring to the attention of the management any representations that have been made in the house. Of course, I shall be glad to do that, but that again is a policy that is determined by the directors of the Canadian National.

I do not
know upon what item I can discuss the sale of Canadian National property, for instance, to private individuals.
There are a number of items dealing with Canadian National Railways farther on. Perhaps, if my hon. friend allows me, I could find one and indicate it to him.
I have been looking through the estimates, but I do not see any item that would entitle me to discuss the sale of C.N.R. property.

There is no particular item dealing with the sale of property by the Canadian National Railways, because that is done by the railway itself. It might have been brought up under the discussion of Canadian National matters-perhaps the last of the railway items. Then there is an item dealing with Canadian National steamships subsidy, and if the house has no objection the hon. member could deal with it then. I do not want to interfere with my hon. friend.
It is only about two sentences.
Well, go ahead.

What I had reference to was the sale of two properties in Point Edward, which is adjoining Sarnia, on the St. Lawrence seaway project. I mention this because quite evidently something is wrong somewhere. I have a return here described as sessional paper 202 under date of May 4, 1953, which indicates that one property was sold for one dollar, and other considerations, and the name of the purchaser is mentioned in the return. The reason I mention that is that the property, I understand, was resold the other day for $50,000. What the other consideration was-I have an idea what it was, and no doubt the minister has an idea, too-
No, I have not the slightest idea what it was.
I think the house should know more about it-*
Now just a minute-
-because that is ridiculous.

I mentioned to my hon. friend that this was not the place to discuss real estate concerning the Canadian National Railways. I thought he was going to ask a simple question. I am not familiar with any sale of land; that is a matter which the Canadian National Railways deal with under their own authority. But if my hon. friend wants me to take it up with them, I will be pleased to. However, I have no knowledge of it, and I cannot speak about it with any degree of authority. So if this matter is of some significance, I wish the hon. member would not bring it up now. If he would give me the return, I will do what I can.

That is all right. I do not expect any minister in a department to be familiar with everything that takes place under his jurisdiction. When the minister is inquiring about that, I wonder if he would inquire about a sale for $10,500 mentioned in that same return. I will not mention the name of the person involved. I understand he was asking $60,000 for it.
I shall be glad to.

Item agreed to.
Hudson Bay railway-
463. To provide for the difference between the expenditures for operation and maintenance, and revenue accruing from operation during the year ending March 31, 1955, not exceeding $425,000.

This has to do with the deficit of the Canadian National Railways, payment for which is asked by parliament. I would direct the attention of the committee to the subject of the Hudson Bay railway, with particular reference to some suggestions that might be effected which would result in a greater income for that railway, which has been a matter of interest to me for many years. I visited the railway as far back as 1926, at Port Nelson, and then later, in 1931, I made the first trip to Fort Churchill.
I intend to speak particularly about storage capacity for wheat at Fort Churchill, and to express the appreciation which all of us in western Canada who are interested in this route-and that applies to everyone-feel for the fact that the storage capacity will be doubled during the current year to a point where it will accommodate 5 million bushels.
During the past year there has been a greater use of the Hudson bay route than ever before, the export of wheat from that point reaching 10,800,000 bushels. With the new facilities in prospect I believe it will

not be long before the export of wheat from Fort Churchill will amount to 20 million or 25 million bushels.
In the last season 31 ships called at the port, almost all with empty holds in their trip from east to west. The total amount of imports, in actual tonnage, stood at 2,790 tons, which is less than one shipload. I feel everything possible should be done to encourage east-west traffic over the Hudson bay route. This should be done through advertising to a greater extent than ever before-through Canada House in London and other government facilities in various parts of Europe. An effort should be made in this way to point out the savings that can be effected by shipping through Hudson bay, so that to the greatest possible extent the Hudson Bay railway may be used, as it should be used.
For years there were many who contended that to use that route would be a dangerous expedient. The Hudson's Bay Company used it for over 260 years, and suffered little loss from the dangers that have been conjured up in recent years.
By way of personal reference, my own great-grandparents came through Churchill in 1812 with those groups of settlers who came to the Red river at that time. They found none of those difficulties of navigation that have been referred to in such fearsome terms within the last 25 or 30 years, when we in the western provinces have demanded the extension of the use of the facilities there.
It has been established in recent years that navigation is now comparatively safe -and when I say "comparatively safe" I mean when compared with navigation into the other great ports of our country. True, the port has a short season; but even in the face of that short season during the year 1953 the port was idle only 11 days when it could have been operated to the full.
I feel that while congratulations are due to those responsible for securing added use of these facilities in the last year, further efforts should be made. Referring to a railroad in British Columbia a moment ago, the minister said that it ended nowhere.
It used to; but no longer.

I appreciate that; the situation was remedied. When he replies, I would ask the minister to say whether or not an application has been made by American interests not only to build a railway from the international boundary to Fairbanks, Alaska, but also to connect such a defence railway with Fort Churchill and Prince Rupert. The press states that this defence railway is backed by the United States government, and would be intended for military
Supply-Transport
purposes. By linking up with Fort Churchill, feeders would be available to the projected railroad, which those who are alleged to have applied for the right to construct have in mind.
What is needed today, as I see it, is a greater use of the Hudson bay route. That greater use is impossible today, or its possibilities are greatly diminished, because there are railroads in Saskatchewan and through northern Saskatchewan that, while ultimately intended to join with the port of Churchill and the Hudson Bay railway, have not been built. There is a line northeast of Melfort in Saskatchewan. There are also those breaks in the Canadian National Railways in northeastern Saskatchewan and the Beaver river area where the railroad comes to an end. It is the end of the line, and thirty miles distant it starts again. These laps or breaks should be constructed to enable a greater use to be made of the facilities at Churchill and the Hudson Bay railway.
I suggest to the minister that he place before the committee information regarding the courses being taken by the government or by governmental agencies to encourage the use of this railway and thereby reduce the deficit. There is no reason at all why the traffic from the tremendous mining development that is taking place in northern Saskatchewan, as an example, should be excluded from Churchill and the Hudson Bay railway.
In the matter of base metals and uranium, the developments taking place in northern Saskatchewan and Manitoba are such that the mineral possibilities stagger the imagination. According to those qualified to speak, the uranium developments in northern Saskatchewan are such that within a matter of a few years Canada's uranium production will be greater than that of any other place in the world, including the Belgian Congo. Yet, these developments in northern Saskatchewan have no railway facilities available to them.
I ask the minister this question: What consideration has been given to the application made by United States interests? According to press reports, those interests were prepared to spend $446 million on building such a railway line to join up with the Hudson Bay line, thereby adding to the revenues of the Hudson Bay line and indirectly to the revenues of Canada. Second, what are the prospects of reducing the high haul insurance rates that today prevail on the Churchill route? Generally speaking, insurance rates have been reduced, but the haul insurance rates are still exorbitant, and in my opinion unjustifiable. That is the view of an organization which has done much to interest the

Supply-Transport
people of Canada in this project. I refer of course to the Hudson Bay Route Association.
Third, in view of the fact that the wheat that goes over the Hudson Bay railway and into Churchill and thence to the markets of the world is exclusively restricted to that produced on Canadian National lines, I desire to ask this question. Has the Canadian Pacific Railway at any time endeavoured to secure running rights over the Hudson Bay railway so that wheat from those lines might be available to that port? Fourth, has consideration been given among the various departments of government to the wheat board lowering the 1| cents per bushel diversion charge on wheat shipped through Churchill to the end that by reduction of that charge there will be further encouragement of the use of this railroad? Fifth, and this is a suggestion which I think deserves serious consideration-it was made by Mr. W. G. Coventry, the United Kingdom trade commissioner in Winnipeg. He suggested that imports from the United Kingdom to western Canada might be considerably increased if facilities such as Queen's warehouses could be established in the northeastern areas of Manitoba or in Saskatchewan. All of us in the western provinces appreciate the greater use that has been made of the Hudson bay route since my hon. friend has been Minister of Transport.
As I remember it, the first wheat that was shipped over that route was in 1931. By 1935, under the Bennett government, shipments had increased to some 5 million bushels. Then for years those facilities, which are extensive, were almost ignored. Today, however, with the advantages of cheaper marketing that are available, more and more the route is being used. I feel that with an advertising program and with some of the changes made to which I made reference, which by no means are complete, further use could be made of this railroad-and further use should be made of it than has at any time been made previously.
In making these representations to the minister I do not want to go into further detail. Indeed, there are many things that I could say on the subject that might possibly be of some interest, but I do not want to speak at length at this time in the session. I do, however, ask the minister to give the committee, and through the committee western Canada, the assurance that, extensive as has been the use of these facilities during the past couple of years, with the increase of storage facilities at Churchill that are projected for this summer, at the earliest possible date, and I trust within a year or a year and a half, at least 20 million bushels of wheat will be shipped from this port, which will

not only accrue to the advantage of the people of Canada but will reduce or remove the deficits altogether and also increase the return that the western farmers wiU receive from the wheat shipped through that port.

Before the minister replies I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Prince Albert on the interesting and excellent speech he has delivered. Will the minister indicate whether or not a contract for the extension that is to take place in Churchill has been let? Can he give the committee some information as to the number of ships that might be expected in Churchill this summer? Has he information as to the number of cargoes that may be assured at this date?

I thank the hon. members for Prince Albert and Mackenzie for their interest in the Hudson Bay railway, and particularly the hon. member for Prince Albert, who is appreciative of what has been done with reference to the extension of the elevator at Churchill so as to provide for the greater movement of wheat out of that port.
There are a number of matters the hon. members raised some of which fall under this heading and others do not, but I will try to deal with them at this time. One inquiry was about an application which was reported in the press as having been made by some United States interests for the building of a railway from the United States border to Fairbanks, Alaska, and then perhaps join up with the other railways in northern Alberta and northern Saskatchewan. I can tell him immediately that I have no knowledge of any such application. I could not say, however, that I have no knowledge of the latter ever having come up before. This is not the first time it has been suggested that a railway be built from the United States border to Alaska, but I am not aware of any application, and certainly no application has ever been made to the Department of Transport, and I doubt very much if one has ever been made to the government.

May I say to the minister that Mr. Appleby made a speech to the Hudson Bay association in Moose Jaw in March and I have sent him over the clipping in question which contains every detail to which I made reference.

Continuing with my answer, if there was any foundation to this then the project might be carried out in a number of ways. It might be done by way of an extension to the P.G.E. so long as it remained within the province of British Columbia. The application then would not be made here but to the legislature of the province of

British Columbia. If the extension or the line itself went into more than one province the application, of course, would have to come here.
I am not saying I have never heard of it. I have heard of it repeatedly from many sources. But the inquiries I have made lead me to believe that this is not a serious matter. By that I mean there is no substantial foundation to the statement that such a railway will be built. Certainly no application has been made and until one has been made there is no question of giving it consideration.
Now, with reference to the insurance rates, as my hon. friend knows we do not determine these in the Department of Transport. They are, I understand, determined by a committee in the United Kingdom since the ships come from there, and we have repeatedly made representations to that committee in the United Kingdom recommending a decrease in such rates. We have been informed that if we could assist by further aids to navigation consideration would then be given to this. Now, we have done a great deal with reference to improving aids to navigation in Hudson bay, Hudson strait, James bay, at Churchill and all along the route of the eastern coast of northern Canada. We have installed a responder type of radio beacon at one end of Charles island, one at the entrance to Churchill harbour, and also a radar screen reflector. The R.C.A.F. maintains an air-ice reconnaissance patrol in the area which is of great assistance to ships navigating in the bay and strait and, as my hon. friend knows, our own ships such as the C. D. Howe, the N. B. McLean in the past, and now the d'Iberville assist ships from other countries into the straits when the season of navigation opens. We will continue to provide as many navigational facilities as possible and continue to make representations to the British committee in regard to a further reduction in the haul insurance rates.
I am not aware that the Canadian Pacific Railway has endeavoured to secure running rights on the Hudson Bay railway. The diversion charge and its reduction, to which my hon. friend referred, is not a matter which falls within the jurisdiction of this department. It is one that comes under the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
In answer to the hon. member for Mackenzie, a recommendation for the award of the contract for the extension of the elevator at Churchill to the Carter Construction Company, which was the lowest bidder, has been made. A report to council has gone forward recommending the acceptance of that bid.
Supply-Transport
It is expected that the flow of traffic in Churchill will be as good as last year and I hope better. Last year there were some 31 ships and we hope there will be as many if not more this year. They provided for the movement of 20 million bushels of wheat-
I think it was 10-8 million.

I thank my hon. friend for the correction. They provided for the movement of 10 million bushels of wheat, but with the extension it will be possible to handle 20 million bushels. I had intended to add that I see from a statement before me that there is a gradual increase in the traffic over the Hudson Bay railway. The Canadian National Railways tried to divert and direct traffic to the line and I think the position was certainly far better in the last fiscal year than ever before, and I hope it will continue growing.
Not away from Vancouver, I hope.
We aim to provide greater facilities at the port of Churchill and the national harbours board seeks to see to it that there are sufficient facilities to look after the traffic there.

May I ask the minister what effect, if any, the development of the St. Lawrence seaway will have on the shipment of grain through port Churchill? I remember when I was up there two years ago the elevator they had there then had not been used and was empty. Now we are building another one.
All I can say is that the economic studies which were made indicated it would have no adverse effect on Churchill.

When we were discussing the first item the minister stated he would be in a position to make a statement regarding the cost of hauling grain through the Crows-nest pass. Can the minister now make that statement?

I hoped to be able to make that statement but I am afraid I will have to ask the hon. member to accept my explanation at this time. I have here a long statement which has been prepared for me, a small portion of which deals with the compensatory part of the movement of grain through Crowsnest pass. Since the time this statement was prepared I have asked those who prepared it to look at it once again. This statement was prepared some time ago and they have now indicated to me that it would be unwise for me to place it on the record. I hope my hon. friend will accept my explanation. I would rather not put it on

Supply-Transport
the record because it should receive further study. I can reiterate what I said earlier, that there is no question of amending the Crowsnest rates at this time. I hope my hon. friend will accept that statement.

I should like to ask the minister what his reaction is to my suggestion that there be established Queen's warehouses similar to those that have been established in ports in other parts of the world to the end that thereby imports from the United Kingdom might be encouraged. One of our great difficulties is that of these 30 ships to which reference has been made and which came into the port of Churchill during the past season, practically all had empty holds.
During the course of my earlier remarks I asked the minister what was being done to advertise the advantages of this route to the end that on the east-west course of trade a larger percentage of trade would be the result. A moment ago I placed before him -and I know it was through inadvertence that he did not answer-the suggestion made by a highly experienced man, namely the United Kingdom trade commissioner. I should like to know what his reaction is to that suggestion and also to the suggestion that Canada House might be used to a greater extent as a means of promoting interest in this route among Eritish shippers.
My friend the hon. member for Royal asked what the situation would be when the St. Lawrence waterway was established. I made some investigation in that regard, and the best information I could secure on the subject from those in a position to advise was that, even after the construction of the St. Lawrence waterway, as far as the farmers in Alberta and Saskatchewan are concerned the cost of the shipment of wheat by way of port Churchill would be at least 9J cents less than by way of Port Arthur and through the new St. Lawrence waterway. Hence, no matter what is done in connection with the latter waterway, the Hudson bay route will always remain of advantage to the farm producer in Manitoba and Saskatchewan, provided that something is done to encourage the use of that route by importers into western Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I regret that I did not deal with the suggestion made by my hon. friend with regard to foreign trade zones. In effect that is what he was suggesting by Queen's warehouses. I understand that they are the same thing. We gave the matter careful consideration at one time There are advantages and disadvantages to the establishment of zones of that character in the ports of Canada. At one time there

was a strong agitation for such a zone in the port of Quebec, and from the port of Quebec it extended to the port of Halifax. However, we soon discovered that there was as violent opposition to it as there was sentiment in favour of it. We therefore decided to establish an interdepartmental committee- this would be back in 1948, I am told-and they spent some months in considering the problem. They went to Halifax, Saint John, Quebec and Montreal-I doubt if their study included Vancouver-and they gave the matter careful study. Those who were members of that committee were all persons with a great deal of experience in the shipping business.
Of course, I do not remember all of the details of the report, nor am I able to say that the report recommended against foreign trade zones. It was an extremely comprehensive report that set out the advantages and disadvantages. After having carefully studied it, the government did not decide to put these foreign trade zones into effect at any of the ports.
I do not know whether, with respect to a foreign trade zone, the port of Churchill could be considered in any different light from the others. It might be that the circumstances there are such that they could be considered in a different light. I do not know. That is all I would care to say at this time because my memory of the matter is rather vague. However, it is a question that is certainly worthy of consideration. Whether we could act on it or whether it would be advantageous to do so is another matter. However, I will ask our people to see whether they could not give it some study.
With reference to the advertising of that route, may I say that the national harbours board do not advertise one particular section of its system rather than another, nor does the Canadian National Railways. It is true that the railway does advertise summer resorts and so forth in a general way. The national harbours board has a pamphlet entitled "Ship via Canadian Ports", in which is an excellent description of the port of Churchill. It has just now been handed to me by the chairman of the national harbours board. He informs me that it goes to all the shipping agencies in the world. I think that is perhaps one of the proper methods by which to advertise the port. Perhaps I could send it over to my hon. friend.

In this connection I might mention that the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan have published an extremely interesting report on the Hudson bay route

and Churchill. I understand that this volume has been sent to the offices of the trade commissioners in the different ports of the world. I think that what the minister says is quite right, namely that the department cannot very well play up Churchill without meeting criticism from members from Vancouver, Halifax and other ports. However, I think there is no objection to the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan telling of the wonders that this new port offers to exporters in different parts of the world. If any hon. members are interested in this booklet, I may say I have a number of copies upstairs that I should be glad to supply to them.

Item agreed to.
466. Strait of Canso-Transportation improvements and facilities, $9,670,000.

I think it should be said that those in the east are extremely happy indeed with the progress which is being made with the construction of the Canso causeway. I am wondering whether the minister is now in a position to state somewhat definitely when it is expected that the causeway can be opened. I should also like to ask him whether there is any truth in the newspaper story that, when the causeway is opened, it is proposed that the procession be led by the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the minister, both wearing kilts. If that information could be definitely pinpointed and ascertained, I can assure him that this spectacle would be the greatest tourist attraction that has ever been known in the province of Nova Scotia. We should like to have ample warning in order to make provision for the necessary advertising. I would also suggest that possibly that duo should be made a trio and that instead of having two with kilts, there might be included an Irishman with a green plaid in the centre in order to give it balance.

With reference to the last part of my hon. friend's suggestion, let me tell him this. Nothing would please me more than to lead the pipers across the strait in kilts. I would be perfectly at home in a kilt because I am an officer in the Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry Highlanders and they wear kilts. I have worn a kilt on many occasions. Hence if I receive an invitation, I will certainly join with my friend the hon. member for Cape Breton South and any other hon. members who are there. Coming as I do from Stormont and Glengarry, I think I can march to the tune of the bagpipes as smartly as can many of the members here. Progress has been excellent on the Canso project. We are delighted with the contractor and
Supply-Transport
with our consulting engineer. We are delighted with the manner in which the work has proceeded. From the information now at hand it will be January 1, 1955 or thereabouts-
Awfully cold for kilts.

I agree with my hon. friend. He interrupted me. I was not going to say that it would be opened on January 1, 1955. All I was going to say was that it is expected that the progress of the work will be such that by that time we will be able to state when it will actually be opened. It will be early in 1955.
Would the minister tell us whether facilities will be provided for the passage of cargo ships through the causeway? Is there sufficient depth of water?
Yes, provision is being made for the construction of a lock for the movement of ships.

I appreciate the fact that this will facilitate the passage of cargo ships carrying mineral ores from the new mines in the Bathurst area. In view of the importance of these mines which, according to reports now available, will produce over one million tons of mineral ore, and also in view of the fact that on the north shore of New Brunswick we have facilities for shipping twelve months of the year, I wish to mention at this time, in agreement with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Royal, that it is very important that at the earliest possible date consideration be given to having surveys made for the Chignecto canal. If the Chignecto canal were constructed it would cut the distance involved in the transportation of these minerals by at least 400 or 500 miles.

I wish to ask a question about item 465. You were going so fast, Mr. Chairman, that you did not notice me on my feet. The same question has to do with items 470 and 471, and concerns the construction or acquisition of car ferries and terminals. I notice that we are spending a good deal of money. Under item 465 the amount is $1,558,000, under item 470 it is $6,950,000 and under item 471, $900,000. I should like to ask the minister whether in the construction of these ferries that are to operate between the mainland and islands provision is being made for the accommodation of railway cars as well as automobiles.
There is in the one under discussion. The answer to that is yes.

Pardon?

Supply-Transport
With respect to the railway car ferry involved in item 465 provision is made for the transportation of railway cars.

I am informed that in some instances where ferries are being constructed provision is being made for railway cars but the construction is so designed that truck trailers are not able to make use of these ferries. One instance of that was drawn to my attention. If that is so, I think it is a very bad policy. Now that it has been drawn to the minister's attention I would ask him to see to it that when ferries are being constructed to service these particular areas accommodation is provided not only for railway cars but also for trailer trucks. I would think that would be a very important means of transportation for the people in these areas.

My hon. friend is right in his assumption that it is important to provide for the movement of trucks, but he is absolutely wrong in his assumption that provision is not being made. On the contrary, provision has been made in this car ferry for the movement of trucks. Another car ferry is being built by the government for service between Wood Islands and Caribou, and it is exclusively for the movement of goods on trucks. Provision is made for trucks on the Port aux Basques-North Sydney ferry and the Yarmouth-Bar Harbor ferry. These are not car ferries at all but provision is made for trucks. A substantial number of trucks can be carried on these vessels.

I am very glad to hear the minister say that. I should like to tell him that I had information that in one instance no provision had been made and it was necessary to reconvert the vessel afterwards. Provision had been made for railway cars but the ferry was so constructed that trailer trucks could not make use of it. In that particular case it was reconstructed. I am very pleased to hear the minister say that from now on that is not going to be the case and that special recognition is given to trailer trucks on these ferries. I am sure the trade will also be pleased to hear that.

Item 466 has to do with the causeway across the strait of Canso and the amount of the vote is $9,670,000. One end of the causeway will be in my constituency. I want to ask a question or two. When the causeway was first mooted no doubt the department had an assurance of the probable cost. Since then tenders were called for and contracts were let for the rock fill and the lock. I should like to ask the minister how the

estimates compare with the contracts that have been let for the work that is being done.
While the minister and his officials are getting those figures, perhaps he might listen to my other question. What is going to be done with the scores of employees, married men who own their homes in the towns of Mulgrave, Point Tupper and Port Hawkes-bury, who are employed at the present time on the ferries running between Mulgrave and Point Tupper which carry the trains across from the mainland to the island of Cape Breton? The moment the first train crosses the causeway these men will be out of a job on the ferry boats running between the points I have mentioned. There are some men employed on the railway in the running trades as conductors, brakemen, engineers, firemen and so on who will probably be well taken care of even if they have to deadbeat it back and forth from Sydney to Stellarton, Truro and other places, but the men who are employed on the ferry boats will be out of work the day the first train crosses the causeway.
It is not hard for any of us to imagine their worry now as to what is going to become of them when the causeway is completed and the first train crosses it. This is not the case of an act of God. It is not the case of a mine petering out. This is an act of man. It is an act of parliament, if you want to put it that way. I think some consideration should be given to these men, and probably it already has. However, I should like to know something, and they would also, about what is in store for them when the causeway is completed. They will be out of a job overnight. Where do they go from there? Those are the two questions I want to ask the minister.
Frankly, the third question I should have put earlier, and that is I understand the expenditure on this job was divided between the dominion government, the Nova Scotia government and perhaps the Canadian National Railways. Could the minister inform me as to that division?

Dealing with the first question, the matter of the rock fill on the causeway itself from the mainland to Balache Point, the estimates of the department were higher than the amount of the contract itself. I have not with me the exact amount, but I put it on Hansard when I introduced my estimates earlier.
Now with reference to the second question, that is a very difficult question that my hon. friend raises and one which I am sure will be of particular interest to him and

his constituents. It is not an easy one for me to answer because it is not one that entirely concerns the Department of Transport although it interests our department. My hon. friend will perhaps recall that when the first work on the causeway was begun I, together with the late premier of Nova Scotia, saw a committee from the port of Mulgrave, Port Tupper, and I believe Port Hawkesbury.

I was
with you at the time.

I was going on to say that they were introduced by the hotn. member for Antigonish-Guysborough. At that time it was thought that the whole matter should be given careful study by reference to some committee. It was thought that Nova Scotia might give consideration to the establishment of some industry in that area, and that we might communicate with Canadian National Railways and other interests to ascertain how many employees could be cared for when the causeway work was completed.
Now it is certain that the Canadian National Railways, after the discontinuance of the ferry between Port Tupper and Mulgrave, will be able to take care of a number of men; that has been ascertained. I think I have communicated that by letter to the late premier of Nova Scotia and perhaps to the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough; I am not sure. Then, there are a number of men whom we in the Department of Transport will be able to place on the locks. I am afraid, however, we will not be able to take on all of those who will be let out, but I can assure my hon. friend that those who are interested in the problem, the Canadian National Railways, the Department of Transport and any other government department, will give careful consideration to the finding of employment for those whose employment will disappear.
Now, the last question, the division of the cost of the railway diversion, the locks and the causeway, I shall have to get that information and put it on the record.

Item agreed to.

This item covers the construction of an auto-ferry vessel for service between Wood Islands, Prince Edward Island, and Caribou, Nova Scotia. Can the minister give the committee some information as to when it is expected this ferry will be completed and ready for service, what its capacity will be, and if any arrangements have yet been made as to who will operate it?
Supply-Transport

The decision to build this ferry, as my hon. friend knows, was due to a substantial increase in the traffic between Caribou and Wood Islands. It was decided that the vessel should be allocated, and I am informed that it was given to the Pictou shipyard. It will be ready for service about the last half of 1955. This same item covers the construction of a ferry to operate between Yarmouth and Bar Harbor. I notice that the details on page 536 show that $1 million has been spent on the construction during the fiscal year 1953-54, and it is estimated that $4,100,000 will be spent during this fiscal year. I wonder whether the minister can give us a breakdown of that $1 million. It will be noticed that in the details it is shown so much has been actually expended up to December 31, and then the balance is estimated for the remaining three months of this fiscal year, but that breakdown includes the total vote for all three ferries. One does not get a picture of this $1 million, as to how much was actually spent up to December 31 and how much was estimated would be spent from December 31 to March 31.
The reason for asking this question, I think the minister should know and if not I can tell him quite frankly, is that there have been many disturbing rumours as to the exact course of construction of that ferry. In May of last year we had a provincial election during which we saw pictures of this boat sailing serenely around a full page advertisement. She was travelling at full speed, and had a bone in her teeth and was apparently making fifteen knots in quite rough water. Only $1 million was spent last year, and many people in the province would like to know where this matter stands, whether the ship will be finished this year or what time next year. I know if the minister makes a statement on it, people will accept it. I would appreciate it if he would give me a breakdown of that $1 million and also tell us when, in his opinion, she will be completed and in operation.

I thank the hon. member for the confidence he has in any statement I would make; I certainly appreciate that. The item is for the construction or acquisition of auto-ferry vessels, as detailed in the estimates. There is a provision for $4,100,000

How much of the $1 million was actually spent?

The auditor with me now tells me he has not the amount, because the figures for the audit of 1953-54 are not ready. But perhaps I can get something more definite for my hon. friend and give it to him later. I do not have the details with me now.
The total figure was given, and I thought the minister would have the breakdown.
I am afraid I shall have to get that information for the hon. member, if I may.
With reference to the Wood Islands-Caribou ferry, I would like to know what the capacity of the new boat will be.

The vessel will have an overall length of 345 feet, a speed of 18|- knots; it is designated to make one round trip a day, and has a carrying capacity of 600 passengers; and with its two automobile decks it has a total capacity of 300 cars. It is arranged to handle trucks and buses on the lower deck.

I notice this item has to do with the provision of auto-ferry vessels. Making a comparison of the details given in the estimates I notice that they cover the provision of auto-ferry vessels on the Atlantic coast. I felt I would like to rise and draw to the attention of the minister that at the present time we have another coast in Canada, and that we have developing there a serious situation in connection with the provision of auto-ferry transportation, particularly to some sections of Vancouver island. While I am not rising to suggest that the federal government should necessarily assume responsibilities to the extent that they have been assumed on the eastern coast, I do feel there are some aspects of this problem to which the minister and his department should give serious attention.

When we were discussing the first item of the minister's estimates I did attempt to draw to his attention some of the problems existing at the present time in connection with providing terminal facilities for autoferries, and expressed the hope that at least to that extent his department would consider developing a policy that would overcome some of the difficulties now existing.
So as to complete the general picture as I see it, calculations I make would indicate that for the Atlantic coast of Canada provisions in the estimates by way of operating deficits and subventions seem to total $7,810,725, whereas, so far as I have been able to discover, for the Pacific coast of Canada at the present time we are being asked to provide the modest sum of $345,000.
I am not rising in my place to ask that the amount for the Pacific coast be increased to equal that for the Atlantic, or anything like that; but I do feel the situation is one concerning which the Department of Transport and the federal government could take effective action, if they would. If I were going to put my remarks in the form of a question to the minister I suppose I would ask him whether if Vancouver island were to revert to the status it once had, when it was a separate entity from British Columbia, the federal government would then be willing to consider accepting some of the responsibilities, which apparently they do accept in respect of another island described, so the easterners tell me, as "the island" on the Atlantic coast, just as we term Vancouver island "the island" on the Pacific coast.
The minister will understand I am not suggesting too seriously that Vancouver island should secede from the province of British Columbia merely to be eligible for benefits under confederation that do not exist at the present time. Nevertheless I do hope the minister will give some indication that he is prepared to consider the transportation problem of the British Columbia coastal area.

The minister is always prepared to give consideration to transportation facilities, no matter where they are. But I have to draw to the attention of the hon. member the fact that the position is somewhat different on the Atlantic, because of the terms of confederation. There is a clear indication that the terms of union of Newfoundland with Canada stipulated that Canada would build this ferry service. There was also a clear indication, or certainly there is some indication

and there could be a debate on that-as between Prince Edward Island and the mainland, and the transportation facilities offered there. There can be

no doubt that we have assumed, under the constitution, and I think rightly so, that there was an obligation on the part of the federal government to provide at least a link between Prince Edward Island and the mainland; and that covers two, if not three of the car ferries mentioned in the estimates.
The matter my hon. friend has mentioned has reference, too, to a lack of facilities in certain areas. That would have to be determined by the maritime commission, which is charged with the subsidization of steamship services. They recommend to the government-and I hope I am not inviting debate on the matter. But I think there is a distinction to make between the two.
You are on very safe ground.

I would not want my hon. friends from the west coast, or the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, to think that his area of the country is being overlooked. It is not. But the consideration has to be in one case by way of subsidy, and in the other by way of the fulfilment of a commitment. And I hope he will not take from that any suggestion that we are not anxious to give sympathetic consideration to any application made for additional transportation service on the west coast, or to and from Vancouver island.

I have no desire to provoke a debate, but I could not allow the minister's remarks to go by without making the observation that the provision of transportation facilities was also a term of entering confederation at the time British Columbia entered. The minister will be aware that there has been a controversy, perhaps more of historical than of practical interest, over a great many years as to whether those terms were fulfilled with respect to the provision of transportation and communication with Vancouver island.
At one point there was the suggestion that the obligation was to build a railway across the strait of Georgia. If the minister could solve that problem of course he would be a wizard. I mention it because there is a certain similarity in the provision of communication with British Columbia and Vancouver island, which most certainly was one of the promises on which British Columbia came into confederation.

I have one more question. I understood the minister to say a few moments ago in answer to my question-I forget the term he used-that the ferry would be completed in October. Just what is meant by that? Does it mean that the ferry will be in commission then or launched then? Just

what does he envisage by the term "completed"? When will the ferry be in operation?
My understanding is that it will be in operation in the fall of 1954.

Item agreed to.

In view of the fact that a substantial number of Canadian ships have gene off Canadian registry in the past year, I wonder why this item has not been cut more than it has. $20,000; the McLean, $20,000; the Port aux Basques ferry, $25,000. With respect to strengthening them for defence, that is rather difficult for me to answer. Is all this money then for degaussing, rather than for strengthening the ships in order to equip them with guns?
None of this is for strengthening these ships. It is all for degaussing.

The item then is somewhat misleading. It states:	"Strengthening for
armament."

I have a breakdown here. Yes.

I understood that money had been spent.
No.

The question I was coming to then was this. In regard to the ships which

475. Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships, Limited-to provide for the payment from time to time to the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships, Limited (hereinafter called "the company") of the amount of the deficit occurring during the year ending December 31. 1954, in the operations of the company and the vessels under the control of the company, as certified by the auditors of the company, and upon applications made by the company to the Minister of Finance and approved by the Minister of Transport, not exceeding, $581,000.

Mr. Chairman, this is the
item which provides for a deficit in the operation of the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships and the estimate for this year covers an amount of $581,000. There was no preceding item. As I said during the discussion on the opening item the other day, I hope the minister will see his way clear to assist in encouraging the company to expand the operation of these steamships so that a better and more regular service than the one now in operation will be provided.
Other instances could be given, but the instance to which I referred the other day dealt with the possibility of shipping goods to Venezuela. Farm products from the maritime provinces could be shipped, and provided we had a refrigerator service on a regular basis there could be a tremendous expansion in the export of such goods. Venezuela alone will buy thousands of cases of eggs a week from the maritime provinces. Yesterday when the Minister of Trade and Commerce was speaking on the excellence of the trade commissioners service-and it is an excellent one

I recalled the fact that one of his trade commissioners was in the Annapolis valley, which is the valley, of course, of Canada-

As I say, it is the valley of Canada. I hear some voices raised, and I presume it is in approbation. This trade commissioner was down in the Annapolis valley with assured markets, so he said, for over four thousand cases of eggs a week. I know that this is not a matter with regard to which one can urge that the whole trade be revolutionized overnight. However, I want to impress upon the minister the importance of this service. If he is going to cut down deficits, I think perhaps the further expansion and extension of capital expenditure in providing additional service will ultimately result in greater revenue and possibly the obliteration of deficits entirely.

Before the minister replies, I should like to reiterate the words of the hon. member who has just taken his seat with regard to the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Limited fleet. I appreciate the fact that the operations of it were thoroughly gone over in committee. However we in the maritimes notice that there seems to be a fairly pessimistic attitude about the future of the fleet. I do not think it is in keeping with any good sound business plan for any company that the government and their officials should take this attitude. Recently some sort of announcement crept into the newspapers that a year or two might see the discontinuance of operations entirely. I recall that the minister quickly denied this report in the house and we were appreciative of that fact. But as the hon. member who spoke previously has just said, if you are going to operate any company you must make plans for the future. You must have some new ships, and I suppose new refrigerator service and others, in order to keep this worth-while trade with the West Indies and Caribbean.
A short while ago I questioned the minister and he assured us that the eight ships-I think that is the number-that are still in service in the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Limited fleet are going to be continued in operation for at least another year. I sincerely hope that every effort will be made to keep them in operation. I also hope that the policy-whether it be right or wrong-that the government has with regard to the merchant fleet generally in Canada will not in any way creep into the policies and considerations with regard to

the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Limited fleet itself. I hope that the fleet will be considered on its own merits as a necessary investment for the services that have been built up and which mean a great deal to us in the maritimes.

Before the minister answers I might make one observation. I was not on the committee that went into this matter in detail, but my perusal of the annual report would indicate to me that it might be well to consider putting into service vessels similar to the "Lady" boats that were taken off last year. I am sure they were taken off principally because they were becoming a bit aged and because they were not economical to operate.
They were not patronized.

From my perusal of the annual report it would seem to indicate that the deficit was caused by the cessation of operations of those two vessels. It is indicated in the report that the charter revenues decreased by over $600,000 because those two vessels were taken out of service. I was wondering whether or not they were operating at a profit instead of as the minister has indicated on several occasions. From the report, to a layman-and I include myself- it would appear that these boats were paying. The report says:
Freight revenues amounted to $4,336,008, showing a decrease oi 25-3 per cent. This result was mainly due to a decline in volume and a substantial drop in rates on northbound cargoes of raw sugar, and to the cancellation of six voyages . . .
Passenger revenues were reduced from $869,400 to $132,823 mainly due to the withdrawal of the two remaining "Lady" vessels from service at the end of 1952.
The account given in this report clearly indicates that the reduction in revenue was because of the discontinuation of this service. Whether it was because they were refrigerated and carried additional freight which made up some of the profit, I would not know. Can the minister explain the situation?

As the committee knows, this vote was considered at more than usual length this session before the committee on railways and shipping, and the president of the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Limited dealt fully with this whole subject. First let me say that the company operates eight ships, three diesel-type refrigerated vessels and five non-refrigerated cargo vessels. Operating revenues from the operations during this financial year were $4,945,000 whereas operating expenses were $5,200,000, leaving a net operating loss of $280,000, and when you add interest on bonds and interest on government loans, it makes the estimated income deficit $581,000.

The "Lady" boats were withdrawn because they were not profitable. They were withdrawn also because they were becoming obsolete and, as the president explained, because people are now going to the Caribbean and to the West Indies by plane rather than by ship because of the great saving of time. They were withdrawn also because it was necessary to spend substantial sums of money on them. It was felt that in view of the revenue which was derived from the "Lady" boats as opposed to that derived from the freighters, the time had come to dispose of the others.
This picture, I realize, is not good, but I think it is exceptional. I do not think we shall have a repetition of this situation. I think the potential for trade with the West Indies is great; in fact, it is tremendous. It is unfortunate that the movement of cargo has not been greater between our maritime ports and the British West Indies. I think the sterling question has had a great deal to do with the matter. I again repeat that I believe this is an extreme situation which should not repeat itself this year. For that reason I made a statement in the house which I hoped would allay the fears of anyone that the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Limited were thinking of withdrawing their ships. There is certainly no present intention of doing that. I am hopeful that trade will increase. In fact, the Minister of Trade and Commerce indicated to me some time ago that there was a fairly clear indication that it would increase during the course of the year
I can sum up all the remarks I have to make by saying that the whole position will depend on the operations. If business increases there will be no need for even thinking of withdrawing this service. It is pointed out to me now that the result of operations at the end of April this year as compared with that at the end of April last year is better by about $100,000. I therefore think we can look with some degree of optimism to this trade. I know that the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Limited are not at all anxious to withdraw the service. They are most anxious to have it continue and they are hopeful that the trade will increase.

I might say that I am not a bit critical. I only hope they do continue to operate even if they have to do so at a loss for two or three years because I think eventually they will win. When the sterling question is settled there should be increased trade with the West Indies. As was suggested by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, if several of the vessels that are not refrigerated were refrigerated
Sup p ly-Transport
they could take agricultural products from the maritimes to South American ports. I think that would possibly be one method of solving the difficulty. But I do hope that the service is continued and even expanded regardless of whether they have to operate for several years at a loss.

In some instances that is quite a help.
