Item agreed to.
Air services-
Airways and airports-radio aviation services-
480. Administration, operation and maintenance, $5,749,559.

I should like to make a few general references having to do particularly with administration, operation and maintenance. They concern the need for the development, construction and maintenance of airports in the northern part of our country. I want to thank the department for what is being done in northern Saskatchewan, particularly with respect to the construction of an airport at Prince Albert in my own constituency. In saying that I feel that further development should take place in northern Saskatchewan and in general in the other northern areas of our country where mineral developments are taking place that are great in their extent and tremendous in their possibilities.
One of the main means of securing northern development and the utilization of our natural resources in that region where there is no railway, lake or railway transportation is through the medium of airways. I think it is proper to say that to develop the resources of the north requires air transport at reasonable prices. The air policy of our country was enunciated in 1937, and the conclusion to which the Edmonton Journal has come, after examining air transport in general in a series of articles, may be summed up in these words which I quote:
Our standing relative to the rest of the free world has suffered a net loss between 1937 and 1953 and we are far behind the world's leaders.
That is the conclusion of the Edmonton Journal following a series of several articles dealing with this very important matter. I suggest to the minister that in order to assist northern development a policy greater than anything we have had in the past should be

launched, with particular reference to the provision of facilities for the landing of aircraft, the shipment of supplies and the provision of passenger transport into the north. I believe that the present costs of travel and of transport deserve to be reconsidered in the light of present circumstances, and that the federal government can make a major contribution towards making air transport economical by expanding to the widest possible degree the building of airports in the north and by providing all the ancillary services which would necessarily be required in addition to that development.
I am not going to talk of other provinces in particular, but of the province of Saskatchewan. I feel that having regard to the developments that are taking place in northern Saskatchewan immediate consideration should be given to the improvement of airport facilities at Lac la Ronge, north of Churchill, and also at Uranium City so that a greater degree of air service will be provided there than has been the case heretofore.
I believe that northern development is being held back by the lack of the necessary air facilities as well as air services at reasonable rates. I am not going into the costs of travel on this occasion for that would take longer than the committee would desire to hear me at this time. But I do point out that something should be done to assure that our airport facilities are made as efficient as the needs of modern development require; that they should be expanded and their expansion would give the opportunity for extended mineral development in those portions of our country where rail and water transportation is not available. Such a policy would not only pay large dividends in increased development but it would also provide the basis or the nucleus for the preservation of our defences in northern Canada.
In so far as transportation rates are concerned I think that the air transport board should make a thorough review of the northern rate structure. The first thing the government should do, as I see it, is to provide the airport facilities in the north to a greater extent than heretofore. Something has been done, that is true. Much more remains to be done. Secondly, I feel that there should be, as I said a moment ago, a review of the freight rates structure. The Trans-Canada Air Lines and Canadian Pacific Air Lines make a great contribution to our country. The Canadian Pacific Air Lines are doing a tremendous job in facilitating the opening of the northern outposts of our country, and in particular those areas in which mineral developments are taking place and which will expand to a far greater extent in the years that lie ahead.

I believe that today passenger rates and air freight rates are too high. If it is a matter of facilities and airports that is contributing to that, then the federal government I suggest has a responsibility to render to the highest degree possible the efficiency of the airports.
Let me give you two or three examples, Mr. Chairman, so far as passenger rates are concerned. The rate from Edmonton to Yellowknife is $80, and for almost the same distance from Edmonton to Brandon it is $50. The rate from Edmonton to Beaver-lodge is $64 compared with $30.50 to Regina, an equivalent distance. I am making all allowances for the differences in facilities on the airways that prevail in the southern portion of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. These rates would appear to be not encouraging to the development of the north. Furthermore, in regard to passenger rates it costs more to travel in Canada when one travels by T.C.A. than when one travels internationally. The rate from Calgary to Vancouver is 8-5 cents per mile, and from Montreal to New York it is 5-8 cents per mile. It costs $19 more to travel from Vancouver to Montreal than it does from Vancouver to New York. Those are but examples of a rate structure which I think deserves consideration, and that rate structure, in northern development, is a major element to be considered.
If the rates that are high into the north today are due in part to the lack of necessary facilities that the Department of Transport could provide, then I would think it would be an expenditure paying dividends beyond our present expectations in the encouragement it will give to the exploiting of those resources that are there. At the same time the provision of facilities would be useful for defence should defence be required at any time. I would ask the minister what consideration is being given to the expansion of airports in the northern portions of Alberta, Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec, to provide the opportunities that only the state can provide so that private enterprise may be able to economically enter those areas to expand the development. Great as that development is today, I believe it could be greatly increased and facilitated by a worthwhile expenditure of that type.
I come back to where I started. I suggest that this is a very complex subject, and that it deserves the consideration of the transport board in so far as rates are concerned; that it concerns the Department of Transport, which has done a commendable amount of work in connection with the development of airports in recent years but which has not
Supp ly-Transport
met, to the degree I feel it should have met, the tremendous possibilities inherent in the hidden resources of the northern part of our country. Everything that we can do should be done, and the state has a contribution to make with regard to providing opportunities for air transport.

I should like to make a brief reference to a problem that is quite specific. It concerns the qualifications of pilots, both commercial and private, as radio operators. Radio facilities are of the utmost importance to pilots, whether they be carrying the responsibilities of commercial air line flying or whether they be flying merely for their own personal pleasure or personal business.
I understand that in order to be able to use any radio facilities it is necessary for pilots to be completely certified radio operators. With regard to the qualifications as between the holders of commercial pilot licences and private pilot licences, the requirements are scaled down considerably for the latter. That is, the private pilot does not have to have the broad background of technical knowledge, professional knowledge, meteorology, and the like, that is required by the more responsible position of pilot of a commercial air liner.
It seems to me the same formula might operate for radio operators. If a private pilot is going to use radio equipment to aid him in navigation, or to facilitate communication between air and ground, he usually has a simple set, or one that would be no more complex than the radio found in a home. Or if he uses radiotelephony, it would be as simple in its operation as an ordinary house telephone. It has been pointed out to me that it would facilitate considerably the use of the simpler radio aids available to a private pilot if the qualifications could be scaled down somewhat as they are for other qualifications in flying operations.

Mr. Chairman, between 1942 and 1952 the air traffic at Vancouver airport increased about 14 times. That is a tremendous increase, and is indicative of what is bound to come. I raise the question at this time because in the lower mainland of British Columbia we have so little space available for airport purposes that I think the Department of Transport should begin thinking seriously of taking every available opportunity to be sure that land is being kept for that purpose.
Approximately 10 per cent of traffic at the airport today is of the military type. We have two small civilian airports, one at Langley Prairie and the other at Haney. Let me say that the people at Langley Prairie

Supply-Transport
would like me to bestow their best wishes and thanks upon the minister for including a small grant to that municipality to maintain the airport.
If in this country we follow the European plan of developing aircraft-and I think we are doing it to a degree-there is a possibility of using helicopters on a large scale. I spoke to the president of Trans-Canada Air Lines when he appeared before the committee. Discussing the matter privately with him he said that he thought that if we ever get helicopters that will accommodate 20 or 30 passengers we would soon find them being used between Vancouver, Nanaimo, Victoria and Seattle in the United States.
For that reason and many others, we can easily see that air traffic is definitely going to increase as the years go by. As I said earlier, in the vicinity of Vancouver we have very few sites available for airport purposes. There are certain physical factors needed in airport building with which the minister is quite familiar and which I need not outline here. These conditions leave us in a position where we just do not have many sites left.
One of the most important factors is land. While we have considerable land in the lower portion of the delta, it is not suitable because there is no bottom to it. It is not satisfactory for the purpose of building airports.
One of the most important points is that it is about a 35-minute jump from the city to the airport. That is true of the Sea Island airport, which is being used at the present time.
There is another factor which must be considered, and that is the separation of civilian aircraft from military aircraft, and from the operations of large passenger-carrier types. In this connection I would refer to an article that appeared on the editorial page of the Vancouver Province on May 28. It is headed "Before There's Another Moose Jaw Tragedy," and states:
E.C.A.F. pilot training should be moved away from Vancouver's international airport-the busiest airport in Canada-before there is a duplication of the recent Moose Jaw tragedy.
Airline and airport officials are unanimous that our flying field will become hazardous unless other places are found for training student pilots.
We hope that R.C.A.F. authorities will take steps to remedy the situation before a ghastly accident vindicates the warnings made this week. R.C.A.F. training should be moved to another airport- moved just as fast as practically possible.
There are fields at Abbotsford, Boundary Bay and Comox that would serve R.C.A.F. training needs just as well as Vancouver, whose airport is twice as busy as any other in Canada.
This is not to discount the value of R.C.A.F. training or deprecate the ability of R.C.A.F. student pilots. The point is that it is not necessary to pick

the country's most congested airport to train flyers when there are other fields, just as suitable, within a few minutes flying time.
R.C.A.F. students are flying everything from Harvard trainers to jet fighters and the danger lies in the fact that the student, new to the machine, is so busy keeping it in the air that he can't always give enough attention to keeping an eye out for the big passenger transports.
Before the Moose Jaw crash, Canadian Airline Pilots' Association had written to the R.C.A.F. protesting the placing of R.C.A.F. stations along civilian airways. This complaint is underlined when an R.C.A.F. training station is right at the busiest flying field in the country.
One air expert sums up the situation this way: "The pilot of a heavy airliner, carrying anywhere up to 70 passengers, has a right to feel that he and his passengers can approach a field and concentrate on landing without having to cope with unnecessary hazards."
Less urgent, but also important, is the need to find other places than the airport for private student pilots. In time it will be necessary to consider finding a secondary airport for students, according to the experts.
But the urgent, immediate problem is to move the R.C.A.F. pilot training to a safer flying zone.
There is no other place for the big airliners to go. But there are other fields for the R.C.A.F.
Those fields are established, and I would urge the minister to interview the officials in the R.C.A.F. and the defence department to see if the training schools could not be put in another area. I would urge, further, that he look over the situation carefully, because it is an important one. There were six or seven fields available a few years ago, but today there are only two on the lower mainland that would be acceptable as secondary airports.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Before the dinner hour I had read an editorial from the Vancouver Province regarding the need for another place for the R.C.A.F. airbase and for civilian aircraft other than the Sea Island airport. In 1946, Harland Bartholomew and Associates examined the airport requirements in the metropolitan area of Vancouver. They made certain proposals, and I may say in this regard that their estimates of airport use has proven to be a very accurate one. They proposed that eventually there should be three major airports, one of which should be a military one, one secondary and three minor airports. We have today only the one major airport in the lower region of British Columbia, and that happens to be the one on Sea island. We have two minor ones and a military airport at Abbotsford.

In regard to the Sea Island airport, in the report on airports for the lower mainland we read this at page 18:
At present the Sea Island airport is used by lour distinct types of air traffic, namely, high speed military aircraft, scheduled aircraft, charter and training aircraft. As the field becomes more and more intensively used the hazards inherent in mixing these various types of traffic become more acute. The situation might be compared to an express highway which was expected to handle high speed automobiles, bicycles, pedestrians and tanks at the same time.
I am sure the minister is quite aware of the difficulty, and probably may have certain suggestions relative to it. However I should like to draw this to his attention, since I understand the department has purchased land for further airport development in the Sea Island area. The fact is that it becomes more apparent, particularly since the crash at Moose Jaw, that airports should be farther apart. I would say that the minimum should be five miles, and certainly that five miles separation is not apparent at the Sea Island airport.
Earlier in my statement I mentioned that there were several airports available in the area. These places that are suitable have greatly dwindled until just three are left, one in the region known as Coquitlam, which is in the Burnaby-Coquitlam riding, the second in Delta and the third in the White Rock region. The Delta area is of no use because it has an unsound bottom for aircraft purposes; but in regard to the other two, this same report has this to say:
A site in Port Coquitlam which was recommended by the Bartholomew report in 1946, is still available. However, it is not considered completely suitable because of fog and drainage and foundation problems.
Another potential airport site is located near White Rock, also about one hour's drive from downtown Vancouver. Physically, this is an excellent site. The ground is almost level; tree cover is not heavy; and the area is high, fog free and located in perhaps the clearest and sunniest area in the lower mainland. Runways of 6,000 feet will be possible, allowing it to become a secondary airport.
Now, sir, we have no secondary airport, and the report earlier indicated we should have one. This could be the secondary airport. The report continues:
The only disadvantage, its distance from the Burrard peninsula, would be lessened considerably if a second major crossing of the Fraser and an express highway to the border were built west of the Pattullo bridge. This highway link would reduce materially the time required to reach the airport site.
That area, according to all reports, is the one area that must be kept in mind. I have had some discussion with the minister in
Supply-Transport
regard to this problem, and as late as March 29 of this year he wrote me a letter in which he had this to say:
According to the information I have received, the lower mainland regional planning board of British Columbia made a study of a site at White Rock some time last year and it considers the White Rock area ideal since the ground is high and level and fog free, as you report in your letter. The great disadvantage appears to be the distance it is located from the city. However, as stated in my letter of March 10, we have no requirement for property in the White Rock area for airport purposes.
You mention the Vancouver international airport being located in an area that is frequently subjected to heavy fogs, but I am sure we must agree that, apart from this, it is quite a good location for the larger airlines and, with the improved aids to air navigation, we feel that we are making no mistake in establishing it as Vancouver's major airport.
In regard to fog, I well remember the situation in which I happened to be involved last year, when the Betty Hutton troupe happened to be in Victoria and I, along with the group, was trying to get a flight out of Victoria to Vancouver. The airport was fogbound and we could not get a plane in or out of the airport. Vancouver was fogbound as well, so the troupe never did get out in time to play that night. I am sure the minister knows of many such instances. Despite all the modern conveniences we have in the Vancouver airport, Sea Island airport is quite frequently fogbound, and of necessity we should have an airport that is less subject to fog. For that purpose we have Abbotsford airport which is used considerably in those instances, but for secondary purposes we have no such fog-free airport.
For that reason perhaps he should, and I trust he will, consider taking a second look at this White Rock region. The reason I mention this is that the whole region is building up rapidly. Representations have been made to me, and I am sure the minister must have had them before my time, asking that some definite statement be made as to whether or not his department has ever considered using that particular region for airport purposes. The increased population makes it necessary to prepare to zone a site such as that for airport purposes. It is necessary that a municipality should know these things so that they can stop the sale of land in a region such as that for residential purposes or other purposes; to prepare restrictions regarding the height of buildings; to prepare the gazetting of the various roads to go about such an area and not permit the roads to go through them which would be of no use later on. They should help in this

Supply-Transport
way to facilitate local municipal projects so they will not hinder or impede what is being done in the municipality.
An indication by this department would help. It would help the municipality to establish sites for hospitals and schools and even secondary and arterial highways. The value of property is naturally affected for two or more miles around such an airport, and it would have a material effect I am sure on anyone who is buying property in the area. They should be made aware of the situation.
We are interested in preventing another crash such as we had at Moose Jaw. We are also interested, particularly in my own riding, in trying to establish once and for all whether the department will at any time consider the use of that site for airport purposes because the municipality has been urged to give it up by various aeronautical experts in that region, possibly some of them from the Department of Transport itself. However, as I said, we do not want any accidents similar to that which took place at Moose Jaw, and we do not want an airport located so close to the city as is the case at Elizabeth, New Jersey, where an airliner crashed in the city, or in Seattle where there was a similar air crash some years ago.
I would urge the minister to take another look at the report issued in 1946 which gave examples of many probable sites in that area. It is true that today there is only one site left, but I hope the minister will indicate to the house his views on the suggestion made by the municipality and by me that the Department of Transport ask the region be zoned for airport purposes so that it might be used at some time in the distant future.
Earlier in the discussion I drew the minister's attention to Mr. McGregor's views on the use of helicopters in carrying passengers to and from White Rock and Vancouver. If helicopters can be obtained which have a large enough passenger carrying capacity there is no doubt aircraft of that type could be utilized in large centres across Canada. I would urge that consideration be given to this suggestion because I understand that in Europe today they already have helicopter services in operation between certain points in Belgium, Holland, and Germany, and I believe some of them are capable of carrying up to 20 passengers.
If helicopters are going to be used in the very near future for trial purposes I would suggest that we might well set up a triangle run between Vancouver, Victoria and Seattle. It might surprise many hon. members to know that it takes less time to fly from Sea

island to the airport on Vancouver island than it does to drive from downtown Vancouver to Sea island, even though the Marpole bridge is closed.

Mr. Chairman, mention has been made by the hon. member who has just taken his seat of the disastrous air crash which occurred at Moose Jaw, and I thought that at this stage the minister could perhaps give us a little more information than has been given to the house up to the present time. It is over two months since that tragedy occurred. In the interval certain questions have been asked here in the House of Commons concerning it. The Minister of Trade and Commerce gave a brief report to the house on May 5, and when we were dealing with the estimates of this department just last week on June 2 my colleague, the hon. member for Queens, asked the minister if he had anything to add to that earlier report of May 5. He indicated that he had nothing to add at that particular time. I would think that perhaps now, in view of the general interest the house has shown in this matter, the minister will give us some further information.
I approach this subject not in any spirit of captious criticism but merely with the desire to obtain information such as any person who travels by air would like to have. It may be that that accident at Moose Jaw was one of those million-to-one chances which might not occur again. On the other hand, there may be circumstances in connection with it which would give rise to a change in the regulations to make it less dangerous in the future. It may be that a greater measure of co-operation is desirable between the Department of Transport and the Department of National Defence, both of which are concerned with aircraft traversing our airways. It is for this reason that I rise at this moment to suggest to the minister that he give us some further information.
With the increase in air traffic the public is as much interested in safety regulations for that method of travel as they are with regard to travel by rail or on the highways, and from time to time here we have discussed the necessity for better methods of preventing accidents at level crossings, and better methods of controlling highway traffic. Similarly, with regard to the air, it would be helpful if full information was supplied, so that the public, which is becoming airminded, may feel assured that all precautions are being taken to transport them from one airport to another in as safe a manner as possible.

I do not think there is any need for criticism of one service or another. I do not propose to indulge in that. We have great admiration for the effective operation of T.C.A., and equal admiration for the training program of the R.C.A.F. I am sure everyone appreciates the need for carrying on the programs of the two services at the highest efficiency. Nevertheless, when a tragedy occurs, such as that at Moose Jaw, it is only right that the subject of air safety be investigated, and that the public be taken into the confidence of the government with regard to the measures that may be undertaken to provide for greater safety in the future. If the simple explanation is that this is one of those unaccountable air accidents, then naturally we will have to be satisfied with that. There appear to be rather exhaustive regulations governing aircraft flying in this country. However, I have here the air regulations which go along with the Aeronautics Act and the copy I have is dated May 24, 1951. Perhaps it is not as up to date as it might be. Nevertheless, I notice, according to these air regulations, part VIII, section 4, that they do not apply to military aircraft. The section reads:
These regulations do not apply,
(a) to military aircraft of His Majesty when manoeuvring under the authority of the Minister of National Defence;
That raises the question as to whether there is some system of co-operation between the Department of Transport and the Department of National Defence to ensure that their regulations are in accord one with the other, and that civilian pilots are familiar with the action that may be taken by military pilots and vice versa.
In the report which the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave to us on May 5 I notice that he mentioned that the T.C.A. aircraft was proceeding west on civil green airways No. 1. The minister might let us know what is meant by "civil green airways No. 1". Does that mark out some specified route which is normally available for T.C.A. aircraft and is that airways route, so called green, known to all other operators of aircraft? The minister might also let us know, based on the regulations, something about flight plans at an airport where both civilian and military aircraft are in operation. Are the flight plans of both types filed with the airport control or air traffic control?
Then what is meant in the regulations by, say, a control area which is called an air space of definite dimensions within which air traffic control is exercised? Then there is a control zone which is an air space of definite dimensions within which rules additional
Supply-Transport
to those governing flights in control areas apply for the protection of air traffic. It would be interesting to know the extent of these areas and whether or not aircraft other than T.C.A. aircraft are permitted to fly in those control areas or control zones. If so, under what regulations do they make those flights? Those, Mr. Chairman, are some of the questions that arise in my mind with regard to this matter.
I grant that the minister is placed in a rather awkward position. On May 5, when the Minister of Trade and Commerce was asked as to who might give us a full report with regard to this matter, in view of the fact that three departments of the government were more or less concerned, he placed the burden on the shoulders of the Minister of Transport. I hope that fact will not prove embarrassing to him but I grant that it is a rather awkward situation when other ministers may be concerned. But whether or not the minister now has in his possession the final report he referred to on June 2, nevertheless after the lapse of over two months, one would surmise that the necessary investigation has taken place and that certain steps have been taken, if required, to improve on our regulations. On the other hand, perhaps the investigation so far has indicated that the regulations are sufficient and satisfactory. But in the general interests of the public and in connection with air safety, I would ask the minister to let the committee now have some information concerning this particular problem.

Mr. Chairman, I think the suggestions of most hon. members who have spoken thus far are reasonable ones. The questions are becoming so numerous that I feel I should proceed to deal with them at once before they add up any higher in number. I should like to put on record the names of the consulting engineers on the St. Lawrence seaway, as asked for by the hon. member for Peterborough. They are as follows: Mr. R. A. C. Henry; Mr. M. V. Sauer; Mr. H. W. Lea; Professor J. E. Hurtubise; Lalonde and Valois; Surveyer, Nenniger and Chenevert, and Dr. Pratley,
Then I should like to deal with the question raised by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings when he inquired as to the breakdown of the $1 million in connection with the payment for the Yarmouth-Bar Harbor ferry. The breakdown is as follows: A payment on January 20, 1954 of $498,300; a payment on January 26 of the same year, $498,300; total payments for the fiscal year 1953-54, $996,600, which is roughly $1 million. There is a payment on April 24, 1954 in the

Supply-Transport
amount of $493,300 which is in accordance with the terms of the contract. I should like to amend the information I gave to him then. This contract went to the Davie Shipbuilding company. The contract was signed on November 7, 1952. The keel was laid on July 30, 1953. Launching will take place on November 8, 1954. The delivery date is expected to be May of 1955.
My friend the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra asked for a breakdown of certain information in connection with costs relative to coastguard service. I indicated to him that this was the subject of an investigation made in 1950 and I gave him the figures which I had in my file. I told him that I would inquire about getting a breakdown. As my hon. friend knows, the chairman of that committee is no longer the chairman of the Canadian maritime commission. Another chairman has succeeded him. During the recess he made an attempt to find those costs but was unable to obtain a breakdown. He does not know whether or not they exist. However, if they exist, I will see that my Lon. friend is given them by letter.
The hon. member for Prince Albert made what I thought were some valuable contributions to the debate with reference to airport developments generally, and more particularly having to do with the Northwest Territories and the northern part of Canada. I want first to thank him for his remarks in so far as the department is concerned. I can assure him that they are highly appreciated. I was struck by his statement when he said that we must provide airport facilities in the north to a greater extent. No one agrees with him more fully than I do. I wish we could provide, in the way of facilities in the north, far more than we are providing. In a moment I will put on the record just what we are doing.
The point is that when the estimates for airport development-which includes radio, meteorological and aviation services-come up for consideration, there is always a question as to how much can be allotted to one department as opposed to another. That general amount is determined by the treasury-board under the supervision or the directorship of the Minister of Finance. While we, as a rule, ask for far more than we receive, ; it is important to note that it is not because we are not anxious to provide additional facilities that we do not get all the mongy necessary for their provision. I would remind my hon. friend that here is a program which is by no means a small one. It has to do with the development, as provided for in these estimates, of airports in the north country.

At Terrace, British Columbia, we are providing a radio range at a cost of half a million dollars. At Yellowknife, as I announced on the introduction of my estimates, we are providing a new runway at a cost of three-quarters of a million dollars. At Fort McMur-ray we are providing a new runway at a cost of half a million dollars. At Beaverlodge, which was referred to by my hon. friend as Uranium City, there are a beacon and lighting service facilities at a cost of a quarter of a million dollars. My hon. friend knows that the airport runway at Prince Albert will cost about half a million dollars.
When is that expected to be finished?

This fall. The facilities at Fort Smith include power facilities and new buildings. At Grande Prairie we are installing and building a new runway at a cost of three-quarters of a million dollars; at Prince George a new taxi strip and at Sandspit buildings and power services. If you total these it comes to over $4 million, and that is a very large proportion of the amount in these aviation estimates for airport, meteorological and radio facilities. I am informed that does not include northern Ontario and northern Quebec. There is an indication there that we are not neglecting the north country.
I realize, following several visits I have made there with officials of the department, one to the Northwest Territories, how important it is for the development of natural resources and the development of the whole country to have air services because there are no other services available except the Mackenzie river and its tributaries. We have that matter very much in mind, and I can assure my hon. friend that the Northwest Territories will not be neglected in any sense of the word.
He referred to a revision of the rate structure by the air transport board. That is an important problem. Rates in the air are equally as important as freight or passenger rates on land. I presume my hon. friend had in mind both passenger rates and air cargo rates when he raised that point. The air transport board has now established a working committee with the two major air lines to study the principles underlying freight rates and to ascertain whether, in the light of the recommendations that may come from that committee, it will not be possible to revise the structure.
The hon. member for Brandon-Souris raised the question of the radio qualifications of pilots. There is a certificate of proficiency which must be obtained by both commercial air line pilots and private pilots before they

can operate their craft. In the case of the commercial pilot the certificate is much more stringent, and in the light of what has been said this evening, particularly what has been said by the hon. members for New Westminster and Winnipeg South Centre, I do not think it would be advisable to revise the certificate of proficiency so as to make it easier for a pilot to obtain such a certificate. It seems to me that the regulations of the department, which have been enacted after careful consideration by top technical men, should be maintained.
The hon. member for New Westminster brought up a number of problems which I know he will not expect me to deal with in the short time at my disposal. We consider Vancouver airport as an international airport and as one of the most important airports in Canada.
The most important.

My hon. friend across the way says it is the most important airport. I will not enter into a discussion with him on that. I know other hon. members will have different views, but it is an international airport of great importance. For that reason we consider it as such and we are going to treat it as such. However, many of the problems with which my hon. friend has dealt cannot be discussed by me until such time as we are the proprietors of the airport. We are still discussing the terms of an agreement with the city of Vancouver. We have decided upon the price. The agreement has been revised and approved by our officers and has been sent to the city officials for their approval. I understand from the city that even the principle of the agreement must once again be submitted to the ratepayers by way of a plebiscite. Until there has been a determination by the ratepayers of that city, I do not think any comment by me would be helpful.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre was kind enough to understand my position with respect to the Moose Jaw disaster. When the Minister of Trade and Commerce was asked by the hon. member for Macleod when there would be an opportunity to discuss the Moose Jaw disaster he said: Oh well, when the estimates of the Minister of Transport are up for consideration. I have no objection to discussing that unfortunate tragedy in so far as it concerns the Department of Transport. It is only in that respect that I could discuss it because there were, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated, reports from the Royal Canadian Air Force branch of the Department of National Defence and also from Trans-Canada Air Lines.
Supply-Transport
We received a report, which was an interim report, and that was the report to which my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, referred. I have to say this, that since the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce nothing further has come to light but there is some information I can give to the house which I hope will be of some help.
I know that the house feels very keenly about this accident. Many Canadians travel by the two main transcontinental lines, T.C.A. and C.P.A., and by other lines throughout Canada. It is important that we know that every precaution is being taken to provide for the safety of passengers. I think it can safely be said that this was an unfortunate accident in every sense of the word. The air service people of the department doubt very much if the pilots of either craft saw each other. There is one thing that is certain, namely, that the angle at which the two craft were converging might well indicate that the pilot of the T.C.A. plane did not or could not see the pilot of the Harvard trainer, and vice versa the position of the Harvard trainer at the time of the collision was such that he could not or might not have seen the T.C.A. aircraft. In any event, there is nothing from the wreckage which would indicate that either pilot saw the other.
It is a fact that both pilots were very experienced men. The pilot of the T.C.A. plane had travelled over a million miles without accident. He was one of their older and more experienced pilots. I understand that the young man who was piloting the Harvard trainer was a military pilot of great experience. There is, however, a rule which obtains in the air as it does on the road, namely, that the craft on the right of the other has the right of way. However, that is subject to the exception that if the pilot having the right of way sees that there is an aircraft converging towards him it is nonetheless his duty to move off as quickly as he can. But again I repeat what I said earlier, that I believe from the report that has come to my attention that neither pilot saw the other.
Now then, in order to be helpful to the house,
I should like to say that the report which was referred to by the Minister of Trade and Commerce was an interim report. He stated that the final report was yet to come, and he also stated that a special committee was giving consideration to the reports from defence, T.C.A. and ourselves. To that statement, I can add that the work of the special committee, while it has not yet been completed and I have not before me a final report, indicates nonetheless that the following points of action are being developed:

Supply-Transport
1.	The Royal Canadian Air Force accepts, in principle, and is examining the feasibility of having defined training areas off the airways for use by training establishments located on or immediately adjacent to airways. In addition, it accepts in principle and is exploring the feasibility of requiring training planes to fly below 2,000 feet within airways when travelling from or to the base on the airway.
2.	Hitherto visual flight rule conditions have placed primary responsibility for altitude, course, and the like on the pilot. The civil authorities have recommended and the R.C.A.F. are considering the desirability of parallel civil and military flight regulations which would provide for separation by having flights made at defined altitudes for aircraft crossing airways under visual flight rules conditions.
3.	The committee has expressed its support for the existing Department of Transport program of adding approach control procedures at airport control towers now applying landing and take off controls. This primarily is a matter of obtaining and training additional staff.
4.	Further improvement in reporting and liaison procedures between civil and military channels are to be developed in connection with the reporting of incidents.
5.	On a longer term basis further study is to be given to procedures to be applied in matters of jet aircraft. This is not a new approach, but merely affirms something which had already been recognized and undertaken.
Much of this is technical and again is interim and is under study. I give it to the house, as it was given to me by the member on the committee from the Department of Transport. I do not think it will be possible to deai fully and finally with this matter until such time as the final report is complete. I thought I should put this on the record so the house will know that careful consideration is being given to the matter.

Since the matter of the Moose Jaw air crash has been brought to the attention of the house I have been waiting over the weeks to have something to say about it. What I have to say perhaps is along slightly different lines from what has been discussed before. I am wondering whether the Department of Transport has public relations officers stationed here and there who could more or less represent the department in giving out appropriate information to the press. The Moose Jaw air crash was something that really shocked this nation. It shocked the members of this house, not only because it was an accident that happened between an

army plane and T.C.A., both under the jurisdiction of the government, but also because one of our colleagues, together with his wife, went down in that crash.
I happened to be away for a day or two at that particular time and I read the news in a number of papers. It is for that reason I am asking if the government has any public relations officers. In the reporting of that air crash, I think some of the newspapers went beyond the boundaries of propriety. Such a crash as took place at Moose Jaw, shocking as it was, was a very sensitive thing to publish throughout Canada. I must say that I deplore some of the reporting of that crash. I hold in my hand a clipping and I am not going to say from which newspaper it came, even though I could. I could even give the name of the correspondent, because his name is on the byline. He is reporting what some man said about it, and this is the way the article starts:
Moose Jaw, April 9: It rained human bodies all over. The spinning plane shook them out like a lawn sprinkler. My heart sank and I saw the trapped people were helpless. It was like a horrible nightmare. Men and women fell to earth and rolled up like balls of rags.
Then it quotes who it was who made that statement, an eyewitness. Now that may be so, and it may be the very thing that the eyewitness said. Just imagine the effect on relatives and friends of those who were the victims reading an article like that? How much would it have added to their grief and burden? Here is another report with some pictures and under great big headlines clean across the top of the page:
Bodies drop to earth "rolled up like balls of rags".
Now, here is another clipping that I have where the headline reads:
Identification grim task as sequel to air crash.
Here are a few lines from it; it is in a two column space:
Men shone flashlights into the black charred heap looking for signs of arms and legs. "We have given up looking for whole bodies," one policeman said.
Farther down in the article we find this:
"I ran to the front door. On our lawn there were three dead men and one had no head at all. More bodies were flying through the air.
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me the details we are having now are not related to the item with which we are dealing.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think perhaps the hon. member might indicate how he relates these remarks to item 480 which is before us.
I do not know, Mr. Chairman, what particular reason my hon. friend had for raising that point. I know we do not like to read these things. I am doing this for a purpose.
What is the purpose?

My purpose in doing it is this: I do not want any control of the press. I do not want any censorship of the press. As a matter of fact I would say that on the whole, throughout the country, the accident was reported in fairly well modified and decent terms. But the articles I have just read came from a very prominent daily paper in Canada. I say that I had rather expected that perhaps some highly placed official would have spoken out publicly and deplored that kind of report. That sort of reporting to my mind is very serious, when the nation is shocked, and when the people at home have to bear the burden, and are sensitive to such things. The press have a responsibility, and that responsibility should be met in a dignified manner, and with all reasonableness, having due regard to the sensitivities of a given situation.
As I have said, I thought that perhaps some higher official would do something on that particular point, because they must have seen this, too. As I say, I do not want censorship; but perhaps the purpose will have been served in what I have done. I am not going to ask the minister even to comment upon it. Perhaps, as I say, the purpose will have been served by having brought the matter up in what we sometimes call the highest court in the land. I do appeal to those who are in responsible positions in giving out the news to give out that news, of course, but in such cases as this to give it with the greatest possible care.

I can well understand the hon. gentleman would not, in this particular case, desire to have censorship of the press, because it would have deprived him of the opportunity of relating to the House of Commons the grisly details in the manner in which he has just done it, and in a manner which makes it difficult for those of us who wish to discuss in the light of realistic sanity the possibility of preventing such accidents as this in the future. I think the hon. gentleman, who objects to giving publicity of the kind he has indicated to this kind of accident, has shown more than deplorable taste in rehashing it and giving it additional publicity.
Hear, hear.

I can see no useful purpose to be served in adopting the approach the hon. gentleman has chosen to follow. I had wanted 83276-372J
Supply-Transport
to follow up the matter with the Minister of Transport, with respect to the possibility of devising some regulations which might minimize the chances of this sort of thing occurring again. It probably was the sort of thing that never would occur again, certainly not in those circumstances. But I think we have to look at the situation and try to find out if there are sensible rules which can be devised to minimize the chances.
When to some extent one is dealing in the field of rumour and speculation I appreciate the difficulty the minister is in when he is asked to make a positive statement, particularly in lieu of the fact that he has only interim reports. However, we have heard that at the moment the regulations do not prescribe that the flight plans of civilian aircraft on regular routine operations should be communicated by the Department of Transport at the civilian air stations to the stations of the R.C.A.F., and by them communicated, in turn, to the pilots of R.C.A.F. aircraft. If the information I have received is incorrect, then of course what I shall say in my following remarks would not be applicable. However that is one of the rather disturbing reports we have received.
I am concerned to find out the reason for the absence of the communication of that information, why it is that the flight plans of, for instance, the regular operations of T.C.A. aircraft on regular routes should not be communicated to the R.C.A.F. stations, and by those stations communicated to the pilots or, if you like, just placed on the notice board. Certainly they should be published so that they would be brought to the attention of R.C.A.F. pilots who might be taking off from military fields in the vicinity of the regular air-line routes. And if there is a change in the regular schedule, why should not that fact be communicated to the R.C.A.F. station which, in turn, immediately would draw the information to the attention of the pilots who may be taking off on operational or training flights.
It seems to me that the regular T.C.A. flight schedules might well be posted up on the bulletin board, and instructions issued that no aircraft may take off or return to the field within a reasonable time margin on either side of the anticipated passage of a civilian airliner. And, particularly, if there is a change in a flight plan of a T.C.A. aircraft, or a delay in its flight plan, it would seem to me essential that such information should be communicated immediately by the Department of Transport authorities from the airport at which that new flight plan is filed. It should be sent to the R.C.A.F. station, and by

Supply-Transport
that station communicated to the pilots of the aircraft which may be taking off at that time.

I would remind my hon. friend that this accident occurred under perfect weather conditions, under conditions which, therefore, would bring into operation what are known as visual flight rules. Under such rules and regulations it is not necessary to file a flight plan. It is only in connection with instrument flying that plans are necessary. These plans are filed both by civil aircraft and by military aircraft as well. They are required under the rules and regulations, and the information is exchanged between the centres concerned.
For instance, if a plane is moving from Winnipeg to Regina under instrument flight rules the plan will be filed in Winnipeg. And if there is an aircraft converging on the one moving toward the west, in other words an aircraft moving east, the aircraft moving from Winnipeg will be kept away from the one coming toward him. And, over and above that, he will be in contact with the traffic centre because he is flying on what the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre referred to as the green airway. They are designated by colours and numbers. In this case it is a transcontinental airway, one of the most important and having top priority. The aircraft would be in continual touch, first with the radio range on the airway and then when within a contact radius from the airport, would be in communication with the tower. I think that is the best answer I can give.
Did I understand the minister to say that the filing of flight plans takes place only under conditions where instrument flying is necessary?
That is right.
Surely, even under conditions of good visibility a civilian aircraft is required to file a flight plan, is it not?
He may file a flight plan, if he wishes. Under the regulations he is not required to if he is flying visual.

It seems to me that it should be considered as an additional safety precaution. I had understood that it was already called for. My concern was to find out whether those flight plans were automatically communicated by the Department of Transport, when they are filed, to the R.C.A.F. station in the vicinity of the civil airways along which this aircraft might be flying.
They are, when filed under I.F.R.

Therefore my question is: would there be any insuperable obstacles in the way of requiring them to be filed, whether there was good visibility or bad visibility, and having them communicated by wireless to the R.C.A.F. stations in the vicinity of the route?

No, there certainly would not be. But I presume that is one of the things to which this committee will give consideration. That is why, until the final report is in, I am not able to give any additional information.

The other thing I ask about is whether it is now the practice for the regular T.C.A. schedules to be posted up. Perhaps the minister cannot answer this. That is why I put it in the form of a general observation. It seems to me it would be only prudent- I am told it is not the practice-for the regular T.C.A. schedules to be posted up in R.C.A.F. stations in the vicinity of the routes, and that their pilots should be instructed not to take off at least in such a way as to cross the routes at a time, or within a reasonable margin of the time, when a T.C.A. plane might be expected to be in that vicinity; and, particularly if there is a change in the schedule of the T.C.A. aircraft it should be immediately communicated to the R.C.A.F. station.
I want to make it clear that what I am saying to some extent is in the realm of speculation, because we have not complete information. I am not trying to be wise after the event and to suggest criticism which perhaps none of us would have thought of beforehand, but merely to give expression to observations and thoughts which have occurred to others besides myself, which have quite general currency at the present time, as suggestions which might help to minimize the possibility of such things occurring in the future.

Is any move under way to have the R.C.A.F. training taken away from these larger airports in the country? The hon. member for New Westminster read an extract from a report about the Vancouver airport and the dangers there from R.C.A.F. training. By the way that danger is more from the reserve air force than from the permanent air force. Statements were made by two very prominent men in the air field. Grant McConachie, the president of Canadian Pacific Air Lines was reported as saying:
The situation is becoming a hazard.

Then, Don MacLaren, who is assistant to the president of Trans-Canada Air Lines- incidentally he was one of Canada's four leading fliers in the first war and has been in the flying field ever since the first war- had this to say:
The first and urgent need is to try and find some other airport for R.C.A.F. pilot training, then tackle the possibility of a secondary airport for private pilot training.
Has the government in mind any plan which will bring about the transfer of training of R.C.A.F. pilots from these large civilian fields?

I neglected to answer that query which was raised by the hon. member for New Westminster, and I am glad the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra brought it up again. Yes, there is a very definite realization of the danger of military aircraft in the vicinity of civilian airports. There are a number of examples

fortunately there are not too many of them. I can think of Vancouver as one and Edmonton as another. In the case of Edmonton, representations have been made over the last few years to move as much of the military traffic away from that airport to Namao as possible, and the R.C.A.F. has assented to that recommendation of our officials. If they have not moved it, they will do so in the not too distant future.
The position at Vancouver is somewhat different. We have asked the R.C.A.F. to try to transfer a portion of the training from there to elsewhere, and we shall continue to do that. I presume our position will be much stronger when we have possession of the airport.

There is one other question on this item. What is the position now with regard to flying over the pole? We have had reports in the last few months of a Swedish line which wanted to fly from Europe over the pole and land in Canada and so on. Then, about two months ago there were reports in the press that Canada had refused to make an agreement with the United Kingdom for certain landing rights here en route to Australia. The minister will also remember some questions were asked in the house in March about the agreement between Canada and Australia. There was some difficulty about Canadian Pacific Air Lines being allowed to fly, I think it was a weekly service, to Australia. They were then on a temporary permit, which was to expire today, I notice by a press dispatch. Will the minister tell the committee what has happened in that situation, as well as dealing with the other two I have mentioned?
Supply-Transport

With reference to the flight across the pole, no application has been made to the air transport board by the Scandinavian airlines to fly a route across the pole. They would have to make an application to the air transport board because I understand it was their intention to come down at Edmonton. The application has not been made, although I understand it will be forthcoming some time because they have to clear with the United States. I understand the application covers places such as San Francisco, and/or Seattle, Edmonton, Greenland or Thule and perhaps the United Kingdom and then on to Copenhagen. I presume before they make their application they want to have their licence or an intimation from the United States that they will get the licence. So far no formal application has been made to the air transport board.
With reference to Australia, it is true that Canadian Pacific Air Lines is flying to Australia on a temporary permit only, and the same can be said of the Australian airline, formerly British Commonwealth Pacific Airways now owned and operated by Quantas Airways, into Vancouver. Both are on the same footing and that is where the matter rests. My hon. friend asked another question?
Yes, about the failure to reach an agreement with Britain.

The question of the British agreement was dependent, of course, on whether the position of the C.P.A. would be affected. The British were seeking a continuation of their route from London to Canada on to Vancouver and the Orient via Montreal and Vancouver, with a stopover at both these places. In other words, fifth freedom rights. The government gave consideration to that application, but it had also to give consideration to the views of C.P.A. and T.C.A. because both airlines would be affected; T.C.A. because of fifth freedom rights at Montreal, and C.P.A. because of fifth freedom rights at Vancouver, and it has not been possible to arrive at any decision by way of favourable consideration of that route thus far. What could be considered would be the route from Tokyo to Vancouver with no rights beyond Vancouver for B.O.A.C., but I understand they are not interested in that. In any event I would not like to go further than what I have said now because the talks are not yet completed. When the British minister of transport left here it was on the understanding that I would communicate with him once again as to the views of the government, once we had given consideration to C.P.A.'s point of view. When we

Supply-Transport
were able to do that the government replied to the British minister of transport and since then we have received no statement from him.
Why was it not possible to reach an agreement with Australia? What is the difficulty there?

That is a rather difficult question to answer. I suppose when a country cannot get air rights in another country it is because that country is reluctant to give them. For instance, if we were asked for certain rights in Canada by a foreign air line and we opposed them straight away because it would have seriously affected both T.C.A. and C.P.A., that country might well say it is unable to reach an agreement with us, but that is because it has nothing to give us, or at least nothing in which we are interested. But that country desires traffic rights here which might affect our air lines. I can only answer the question with reference to Australia in that manner. It may be that Australia feels that its lines will be affected by competition from C.P.A.
But there is a temporary permit given in each case. Why cannot some permanent arrangement be worked out? Why do they have to carry on on a temporary basis?

It is certainly not because we did not try. Our officials spent several weeks in Australia discussing this with the Australians and were unable to convince them that they should grant a weekly service to C.P.A. However, we are still in discussion with them on that.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with considerable interest to the statement the minister made regarding the report of the accident at Moose Jaw, and the changes tentatively contemplated in regard to flying regulations. I asked the minister for a statement on that matter when his estimates were last considered on June 2, and I am very pleased with what he has had to say tonight.
Among the things he suggested should be considered was the possibility of making regulations which would require pilots flying across airways to fly at a certain definite height even when flying under conditions of clear visibility. I think such regulations apply now to instrument flying conditions, and I think it would be a reasonable regulation to put into force. The same result could be gained, of course, by requiring aircraft crossing airways to do so only under 2,000 feet, as the minister has himself suggested.
One factor which I hope will be kept in mind is that for regulations to be satisfactory they must be as simple as possible so that on the one hand they will reduce to a minimum the possibility of such accidents

recurring, but that on the other hand they will be sufficiently simple that they will be strictly followed and will cause a minimum of inconvenience to both civil aircraft and the training operations of the air force. With that in mind I think a method can be worked out whereby the possibilities of such accidents recurring can be reduced to a minimum so that they will be unlikely to occur in future.
It has been suggested that the training establishments of the R.C.A.F. should be moved from civil airways. I think that where this is possible it would prove to be an excellent idea, but I think also that if suitable regulations are made and carefully followed it is possible for both operations to be carried on at the same place.

Mr. Chairman, let me say first of all to my hon. friend that I do not think he is quite fair in his statement that the north country has not been treated adequately in comparison with the rest of the country, in view of the statement which I made earlier and which certainly indicates that the Northwest Territories have received a fair proportion of the expenditures in these estimates. Certainly they have received far more than I have ever been able to bring down since I have been in charge of the air service here.
My hon. friend asks for a plan. In reply I would tell him this. To indicate now or at any time what is in the mind of the department is a difficult thing to do. It is as difficult to do that for the northwest as it is for the rest of Canada. It is as difficult to do that for the northwest as it is for Gander or Vancouver or for the main transcontinental airports of Canada. The reason for that difficulty is that air facilities are moving and changing at such a pace that any plan made today might not be suitable tomorrow. Because of the development of the jet and the turbo-prop I think it is quite clear that if we had proceeded to make a plan for any part of Canada having to do with piston engines, we would have had to change it. We had certain definite plans for the transcontinental airports of Canada but they had to be changed considerably, not only with reference to the new developments in aircraft but also in the radio and meteorological fields. For instance let me tell my hon. friend this with reference to the instrument landing systems. They were to be in practically every airport of significance in Canada. I think there are some 24 or 25 such systems. Before long they may all be obsolescent-and they cost a considerable amount of money-because of the coming into effect now of the ground control approach. That is only one indication of what happens in the radio field.
In the field of runways, the situation is this. Where years ago you could land a plane on a strip of gravel you now cannot land the heavier craft on that kind of strip. Runways must be built of asphalt. They must be

Supply-Transport
strengthened, widened and lengthened. That is why it becomes increasingly difficult to make any plan. I know that it will be the aim of the Department of Transport officials to provide in the various parts of Canada all of the facilities they can provide having regard to the money at their disposal. It may be that in certain isolated parts of Canada we cannot get there as quickly as we should like. But the moment that natural resources are developed and assistance is sought by the province, by the company wishing to develop the resources or by air companies using the area, we seek to give them the necessary facilities-with the approval, of course, of treasury board-as quickly as we can. I think that what I have placed on the record now with regard to the northwest is certainly no indication that we have neglected or intend to neglect that part of Canada.

Item agreed to.

I have a question or two I should like to ask the minister on this item. These questions were asked yesterday of the Minister of National Revenue when we were discussing the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and the minister answered that they rightly came under the Department of Transport because they were affected by the licensing authority. There are two questions I wish to ask.
I understand that when radio or television interests desire to construct a transmitter they are not permitted to use what is known as composite equipment. I understand that in Canada no transmitter will be licensed unless it is manufactured by one of the standard equipment companies. In the brief I have in my hand an illustration is given of television equipment that was erected in the United States. Ordinarily it would have cost around $150,000 if purchased from a standard equipment company. The engineers of this particular station erected their own equipment. They assembled it and perhaps manufactured certain parts. They did the job for approximately $80,000. I do not know that those figures would be altogether comparable in Canada, but it means that as long as those who are erecting transmitters for radio or television stations are compelled to go to standard equipment companies and are not allowed to use their own engineers to assemble and make their own equipment they will have to pay a whole lot more money than otherwise.
I should like to know from the minister why that regulation exists. I can quite
[Mr. Chevrier.l
understand that we have to have some sort of inspection service. We have got to be able to inspect the equipment of radio and television stations in order to make sure that it complies with the Radio Act and also to prevent it from interfering with other stations, and so on. But if I may say so it does seem rather harsh to me that radio engineers who are competent to build equipment should be forced to go to the standard equipment companies for their requirements. Their equipment is good and I like to see them do business, but I do not see why the licensing authority should insist that the equipment be purchased from standard equipment companies.
While I am on my feet I might as well ask the further question which I asked last night. Radio and television stations in Canada are not permitted to operate or build what are termed pick-up stations that make use of a pick-up antenna at high level. If they were allowed to do that they would not have to pay for the expensive telephone line services that are required in Canada today. It is a good thing to use the telephone services that are available, but from this same brief I understand that in the United States-

The Secretary of State seems to be aggravated when anyone in this group rises to speak. I will answer the question. It is possible to have shorter questions, but I am not going to have him attempt to take away my privileges in the house.
It is an abuse of privilege.
It is not an abuse of privilege at all. I am explaining my question. We are just taking that much more time.
Oh, the small boy!
