May I deal with the answer to my hon. friend's question about the construction of transmitters and the difficulty of using composite equipment unless it is manufactured by certain standard companies. I do not know that that is exactly the position. In any event the equipment which must be used with reference to these channels must of necessity be of the highest possible standard. There are 3,000 stations and some 105 or more channels which makes it essential that equipment be of a high technical standard and of the best quality. The departmental officials recognize that technical equipment of a certain brand and type is that which is required, and that is why we have adhered to those standards.
With respect to the other question having to do with the pick-up system, if we were to adopt that system it would require far more channels than we have at the present time. As my hon. friend knows, the channels are allocated by international convention. We are short of channels for Canada so that if we were to adopt that suggestion we would have to seek to obtain more channels.

I shall be as brief as I can, but I want to produce certain evidence in support of my argument. I rise particularly to bring a matter to the attention of the house which I have been asked to raise by a number of organizations in my constituency and a considerable number of individuals. I am referring to the fact that during recent years the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company has built a power line from their plants on the Kootenay river along the shore of Kootenay lake over to Kimberley.
Everyone in the district recognizes the advantages of the power line to the district by increasing industrial production and by bringing power and light to communities that did not have power and light before. However, since this power line has been built 83276-373
Supply-Transport
there are hundreds of residents in my constituency, particularly along Kootenay lake between Nelson and Creston, who have suffered from excessive radio interference. I have been present when people were trying to get programs and there has been apparently a zone of interference on both sides of the wires. These old settlers, many of them have been there for 40 or 45 years, are now denied their rights as citizens of Canada to listen to the radio without interference.
This has annoyed these people to such an extent that various organizations have held meetings, discussed the matter, passed resolutions and forwarded those resolutions to me. I have received letters and resolutions from the Crawford Bay women's institute, Boswell and district farmers' institute, Boswell and district women's club, Gray Creek women's club, and a number of individuals who are old settlers in that district. These people are very annoyed at this situation, and I am conveying their annoyance to the minister. Now, with respect to this I did what I usually do, I wrote to the official most directly concerned, and in that case it was Mr. E. Turner, radio inspector at Kelowna, British Columbia, mentioning that I had this complaint and there seemed to be sound justification for it. I asked him if he would have the matter investigated. They had the matter investigated, and I quote Mr. R. A. Coles' reply:
Dear sir,
1.	I wish to report the results of our investigation made at your request to our Mr. E. Turner, radio inspector, Kelowna, B.C., into the radio interference encountered by your constituents in the Gray Creek area from the Cominco power line to Kimberley.
2.	In this respect, arrangements were made for our chief interference inspector to accompany Mr. Turner on this investigation due to complications liable to be encountered. The investigation was carried out between April 7th and April 9th, with the co-operation of Mr. Lee, general manager, West Kootenay Power and Light Company, Trail.
3.	It was discovered that the cause of the interference originated in the transmission line which conveys power at 171 kilovolts from South Slocan to Kimberley. Rather severe interference is caused to the majority of the residents at Crawford Bay, Port Crawford and Gray Creek.
4.	Signal strength readings were taken by our inspectors of stations CKLN, Nelson, CJAT, Trail, KHQ, KGA and KNEW at Spokane and were found to be below the average receivable signal strength.
5.	On this account and due to the fact that we know of no economic cure for the interference from this transmission line, we feel that too much blame cannot be placed on the power company. We do feel, however, and would recommend, that the residents of these areas could overcome this difficulty appreciably in taking their own action by installing a more efficient type of aerial for their receivers and they should obtain advice in this regard from their equipment suppliers.
6.	We regret to have to report to you that no improvement in this situation has been possible

Supply-Transport
from our investigation and that we must place the onus for any action to be taken on the members of your constituency.
Then, after receiving that letter, I wrote to Mr. W. A. Caton, chief inspector, regulations section, telecommunications division. The letter reads as follows:
Dear sir,
I would appreciate receiving a copy of any regulations that cover the question of radio interference occasioned by industrial operations, machinery, household appliances, etc., etc. I would also like any information you can give me concerning the duties of radio inspectors, particularly with reference to radio interference, and what action is taken by your division to enforce the regulations with respect to radio interference caused by any company or individual.
Well, I did not hear from Mr. Caton. Apparently, Mr. Caton is a rather cagey individual and realized that this was something that had to be dealt with at a high level. On May 20, I received the following letter from the minister:
Dear Mr. Herridge:
I have your letter of May 8th, addressed to Mr. W. A. Caton, chief radio inspector, concerning the regulations for controlling radio interference. These regulations were issued in 1941 under authority of section 23 of the Canadian Broadcasting Act, and a copy is enclosed, as requested.
The duties of radio inspectors while engaged in interference work are as follows: The tracing and locating of sources of interference, the development and application of remedial measures and enforcement of the applicable regulations; routine office duties and maintenance in conjunction with the above.
Usually it has been found that the tracing of interference to its source by a radio inspector has resulted in the owner or user taking immediate action to eliminate the condition causing the interference.
Furthermore, in that respect I want to quote briefly from the Department of Transport report, 1952-53, at page 152. There is the heading "Suppression of inductive interference", and I presume that is the same thing about which these people were complaining. It reads:
Fifty-four cars are equipped for the investigation of interference and operate from the permanent inspections offices located in 25 cities throughout Canada. The inspector in charge of each car, with his assistant, investigates reported cases of interference throughout his district, and also monitors receiving conditions during routine patrols. The complainants are interviewed by the investigators, who trace the interference to its actual source. The inspector then advises the owner of the offending equipment how to suppress the interference and, where necessary, conducts appropriate tests.
Then, farther down, the report states:
The co-operation of industry with our radio inspectors has been so satisfactory that up to the present it has been unnecessary to resort to legal action in any cases.

My point is this, Mr. Chairman. I might say the minister sent me a copy of the regulations which I appreciated. In those regulations I see there is provision for a fine if a person does not comply with the regulations and the instructions of the radio inspector. I am not blaming the inspectors. They are doing their duty, but in going through our district I have had it brought to my attention that the radio inspector went into a blacksmith shop in a small village near where I live. The blacksmith had a motor that was causing some interference. He was advised that if he did not correct this situation he would be liable to a fine. There was a man who operated a little carpenter shop and some of his motors were causing interference. He was advised that if he did not correct the situation, he would be liable for a fine. Then, there was Mrs. Muggins with a washing machine or something of that kind that did not work well and she was told she would be liable to a fine if it were not corrected.
My point is this. Why this distinction between a company or large corporation and a small company or private individual? I do not agree with that, Mr. Chairman. My constituents take very strong exception to it, and I should like the minister to explain why a company has to be dealt with at ministerial level, according to regulations, but a small person can be badgered by an inspector. I do not believe that conforms to our conception of justice, and I am always one of those who get their dander up when they see the little person being tramped upon. According to these regulations, it depends on whose ox is gored. I do ask the minister to explain this to us.
I suggest that the people I am representing are most reasonable, but you can understand that if you have lived in a particular area for a number of years and then find your evenings being upset because of these wires you would get upset. I am presenting their upset to the minister. I do ask the minister to look into the matter and see if, as a result of co-operation between the department and the company and the residents concerned, some way may be found to overcome this situation. I do not know enough about the technical aspects of the question, but surely the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company is wealthy enough to provide the small gadgets necessary to overcome this interference. However I ask the minister to have this looked into, to see if there cannot be a co-operative arrangement between the company and the department which would make it possible for these people to receive normal radio reception.
I shall be glad to do that.

Mr. Chairman, when you switched the hon. member for Macleod from item 481 to 482 I think probably I got sidetracked in the remarks I was going to make about item 481. If I can go back that far, I should like to proceed.
We have a condition in Bruce county which is giving grief to a lot of the citizens. Our two radio stations have to change their directional beams at a certain hour in the evening. I had a few questions answered on the order paper some time ago. They were technical questions, but they did answer those questions very well, I think. What I would like to know is this: Is there a chance of permitting those and similar stations to use more of the power for which they are licensed or, if that is not possible, is it possible by international agreement to have some of the American stations cut down their power in the evenings, when it is beamed in our direction.
I can say that I know people who live within twenty-five miles of Owen Sound who cannot get the news broadcast at ten o'clock. In fact, one very reliable gentleman told me that the only night news he can get is from American stations. I am wondering if there are many stations in that position throughout the country and, if so, if there is any solution for the difficulty.

There are not many such stations. The question of power is regulated by the C.B.C. It is the C.B.C. that determines the power a station is to have; and when a recommendation comes to us we can license it only for that amount of power, and for no more. It is possible for a station to make application for additional power, but that must be made to the C.B.C., and it may well be that in the Department of Transport we would object to it because of the international agreement.
That perhaps is the case in the circumstances my hon. friend has described. There are a number of stations which, because of the international agreement, must be given a certain amount of power, and no more. That applies not only in Canada but also in the United States, Mexico and the whole of the North American band. All the stations are bound by a regulating authority which, in our case, is the C.B.C.

Is there any possibility that the power United States stations direct toward the north at night is stepped up to a point higher than our local stations are allowed to direct toward the south? Is there any possibility of that? I am led to 83276-373J
Supply-Transport
believe that the Americans are given more leeway in their night broadcasts than we are in Canada.

I understand there is no such possibility, because they operate in accordance with an international understanding, and international rules and regulations laid down at the conference known as NARBA-North American regional broadcasting agreement. It is possible, as it meets from time to time, to consider this question. When they do meet in these international conventions our people are always anxious to see if stations, such as those the hon. member has mentioned, are not able to increase their power. It is under constant study.

If the stations to which the minister has referred did apply to the department in Ottawa for an increase in power would there be any possibility that the department might give that district closer inspection, and try to relieve the condition.
Yes, there is.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a word or two about the subject introduced by the hon. member for Kootenay West, that of radio interference. This is one of the very few subjects in which I have had some experience. Perhaps society would consider me as one of those people who constitute a real menace-and I do not mean because I am a C.C.F.'er, either. I am a radio amateur operator. As such I have had some experience with radio inspectors and power lines people, so far as this problem of interference is concerned. I believe we cannot cope with what I consider an insurmountable problem of radio interference. A radio inspector can go out on the road and find the cause of some condition that is affecting someone's radio and in a matter of minutes something else interferes. There are motors, X-ray machines and many other electrical gadgets causing this interference.
I believe we are using the wrong approach, and that we will never solve the problem in this way. I do believe however that there is one thing could be done which would go a long way towards solving it. In my view we have to go back to the manufacturers of radio receivers; I believe that is the only solution. That is where we should start, because it will not be solved any other way. So long as radio manufacturers are going to build cheap AC-DC receivers we are not going to have anything but trouble.
But it could all be fixed. There could be many things done to these receivers to overcome the interference. For instance, filters could be installed. I have done it myself on

Supply-Transport
many occasions, where I have succeeded in filtering out noise. But the manufacturer, of course, is not prepared to spend the extra 35 or 40 cents to do this. I maintain that until these manufacturers are prepared to co-operate with the Department of Transport there can be no solution of the problem.
So far as I am concerned, from my experience in the last 20 years it is just a waste of the taxpayers' money to go around trying to find out these pieces of electrical equipment that are causing the trouble. I would like the minister to inquire as to whether there could not be some co-operation by these radio receiver manufacturers. If these companies are going to build the junk they are turning out in the form of AC-DC receivers there can be nothing but trouble. I would like to see some co-operation between the manufacturers and the Department of Transport.
I shall bring the matter to the attention of the department.

Item agreed to.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the fact that this is Friday night and that we have had a long and a rather heavy week. But, as I think hon. members know, the Minister of Transport has a good deal in the way of estimates left, and there is legislation for Monday. I was wondering if we could continue a while on the estimates with a view to disposing of as many as possible of them.
How long a while?
Mr. Chairman, if I might say a word-
Two words.
Ten o'clock.
Oh, pipe down.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order; the hon. member for Macleod may proceed.

Mr. Chairman, one would like to co-operate with the house leader in this respect. Not so long ago the Secretary of State rose and took me to task. I had not been speaking more than a minute before arriving at my question, and he rose and asked why I could not ask my question without making a speech. The hon. member for Kootenay West and others have spoken.
That is their privilege.
That is their privilege and I am glad to hear it. I resented that very much.
Quite right.
The Secretary of State now comes along and wants us to give consent to sitting after ten o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to apologize to the hon. member. I did not mean what I said to apply to what he was saying at all, but it did seem to me there had been a lot of long speeches. This is about the third or fourth day that this department's estimates have been before the committee. If I said anything to hurt the hon. member, I withdraw it at once and I apologize for it.

I appreciate that very much indeed. I do not want to hold up the work of the committee at all, but I did resent that sort of thing. A lot of interruptions came from over here. I will leave it to my leader to say whether he wants to consent to continuing.
As far as we are concerned, we are prepared to go along and help to get through the work of the house.
How long are we going to sit?
How long is a while?

Last night we were asked to sit for a few minutes to let the hon. member for Lethbridge say something. I knew it would not be a few minutes. We have several items left. I imagine there will be a debate on most of them. The Secretary of State may object to members on the opposition side of the house making speeches, but what is it we are supposed to be sent here for? We were sent here to oppose the government, and we cannot oppose the government without making speeches. Probably I am not carrying out my function as a member of the opposition, but we have had a busy week and we are all becoming frayed. Probably we would make more progress by adjourning now and going home.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I purposely stayed out of the debate in order to meet the wishes of hon. members opposite about how long we would sit, because they are accommodating us in going beyond ten o'clock. I do not want to put any restrictions on them. I do think, however, because we have had quite a long general debate on the first item, and since we have covered a good many of the items in other ways as we have gone through the items, there will be less time spent on the succeeding items. I think the minister has been most accommodating in making his answers. We might go on to such time as meets the wishes of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway and perhaps we could get some items through in the meantime.
The minister should not be in too great a hurry to get into the St. Lawrence seaway. We would like to have him around here for a while.

Agreed.

Item agreed to.
Radio aids to marine navigation-
484.	Administration, operation and maintenance. $2,456,995.

I do not
know whether a member has to apologize now even for making a comment. What I am going to discuss does not involve millions or hundreds of thousands, but it does involve something quite serious. A farmer in my riding in the town of Camlachie agreed to sell some 50 acres of land to the department for the purpose of post radio stations. There has been some delay. That goes without saying, since this is June, 1954. It is true that there was never entire agreement on the terms, inasmuch as there seemed to be some misunderstanding between the owner of the farm and the people with whom he was dealing. In the ordinary course of events of closing a small deal these differences could have been overcome in a short time.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I realize the committee is sitting by consent. Might I submit it would be of great assistance to the member who is speaking and the minister who is listening if we could hear the member who is speaking.
Supply-Transport

The small' differences that existed between the purchaser and the vendor could have been taken care of in the usual course of settling a transfer of this size. Anyone who has had any experience in business would appreciate that it could have been done inside of a couple of months. There was some question of drainage and the leasing of the property, and that sort of thing. Apart from all these difficulties, there was nothing that could not be surmounted in due course. I do not mean that it could have been done in an hour and a half but I personally am amazed at this glacial speed in closing a deal involving such a small amount, especially since the department has taken possession of the property and has erected the required buildings on the property, and has had them there for some months.
There were two oil leases on the property that had been on for several years. One was with the Imperial Oil. The release or discharge of that lease could have been obtained in a matter of days. The other one was with someone whose address was unknown. Any lawyer practising in Ontario appreciates that the release or discharge of that oil lease could have been obtained by a court order in a matter of a few days. To me this is a disgraceful revelation of procedure, and there is no excuse for it. There is no excuse for the delay on the part of the department.
As I said, there was some disagreement and the department threatened to take expropriation proceedings. I also appreciate that they agreed he would have the property, and all that sort of thing, for one year. But all these things could have been determined within at least a couple of months. In case there is any doubt in the mind of the minister I want to draw to his attention a letter which I have here from a well-known and capable lawyer in Sarnia, Mr. Knox, who has an excellent reputation and I am sure expedites any matters of this sort that he has in hand. This letter is dated January 15, 1954 and is addressed to the owner of the property, Mr. Howard R. Jackson, and reads:
Dear Mr. Jackson:
I have now received a reply to my letter which was written to the department some months ago.
I do not intend to quote any further. This letter distinctly says that he had received a reply to a letter which was written to the department some months ago. I do not think there is any excuse for that type of business being done by a department of the government and I make no apology for bringing this up. I expect the minister was not acquainted with this.

Supply-Transport
As I said this afternoon, I do not expect any minister of the government could possibly be familiar with every bit of business that goes through his department. That is physically and mentally impossible. Nevertheless, he is responsible for his own department and I am sure the minister, as a lawyer, would regret that there has been such a delay. I think that had it reached his attention months ago the difficulties might have been solved.
I wrote to his parliamentary assistant some six months ago in the hope of having this matter expedited, but now, some 17 months after the deal was initiated, proceedings are commenced to obtain the discharge of these leases. I do not think there is any excuse for that. I am satisfied that if the department carried on all its business in that fashion there would be many regrets, not only in the government but among those in the opposition.
I hope, Mr. Chairman, that there are no other cases such as this in Canada. If this is the way in which the department conducts its affairs in purchasing property from individuals, then I think it is about time it turned over a new leaf and conducted its business in the way it should be conducted, and as is expected by those who deal with the government.

Mr. Chairman, unfortunately there are cases of delay such as this which crop up in the departmental expropriation procedure from time to time. I am not aware of the difficulties which my hon. friend has raised, but my parliamentary assistant is and he has brought them to my attention. The matter which has caused the delay is a cloud on the title. The title, I understand, has to do with certain oil rights of Imperial Oil Limited, and it was not possible, so I understand, for the department to obtain title to the land. I understand, however, that recently the Imperial Oil surrendered their rights. If that is the case then that would involve quite a legal problem which is not very easy to determine, and I would ask my hon. friend to recall that it is not the departmental officials of the Department of Transport who determine the legal position, but the Department of Justice. We seek the advice of the Department of Justice because, of course, they are our legal advisers. I am informed that the matter has practically reached the point where it could be liquidated and I feel, from the information I have at hand, that it should not be delayed any longer.

So there will be no misunderstanding, Mr. Chairman, I might say, with all due respect to the minister, that I do not think any effort was made by the department in Ottawa which was responsible for obtaining this legal advice and having the work completed. They did not make contact with the people who had the leases until some 15 or 16 months after the initial agreement to purchase the property. However, I am glad to hear the minister say that the matter will be finalized very soon.

Item agreed to.
Telegraph and telephone service-*
486. Administration, operation and maintenance. $591,603.

Mr. Chairman, I want to raise again a matter which the minister and I have had under discussion before. This matter concerns a number of members from British Columbia from this side of the house as well as, I think, hon. members on the other side. It relates to the terms of sale of the government telegraph and telephone service in British Columbia to the Canadian National Telegraphs and the British Columbia Telephone Company respectively. There were two matters here of concern to all of us who come from areas which were served by that system. One was the question of the continuation of service to the subscribers to the government service, and the other was the provision for the continuation in employment of the employees of the system.
We had two quite lengthy statements from the minister outlining the arrangements made in both these fields on Wednesday, March 24, and Thursday, March 25, during this session, and I think it fair to say without prejudice -and perhaps I should put in that cautionary word-that with respect to the terms regarding the continuation of service there seems to have been adequate arrangements made to protect the interests of the subscribers to the government system.
We had hoped that the situation with regard to the continuation of employment for the employees of this service would prove to be equally satisfactory. But I regret to say that from information I have received direct from those concerned there seems to have been some bitter disappointment experienced by the men who have tried to make satisfactory deals with the private companies which have taken over the service.
When the minister made his statement on March 24 he informed us that the British Columbia Telephone Company had made

arrangements which were quite satisfactory with regard to the employees of the telephone branch of the system. I refer to his statement as reported at page 3310 of Hansard for that date. But perhaps first of all I should point out that he described to us the terms under which they would be taking them over with respect to seniority in the B.C. Telephone Company employment, and he then dealt with the question of superannuation pension rights. It will be appreciated, Mr. Chairman, that to men of this type who have put in up to 30 years faithful service in the government service, and have now reached the age when superannuation and retirement is quite imminent, the matter of superannuation rights is one of very great importance.

May I ask the hon. member a question? I wish to follow quite clearly what he is saying. Is he dealing now with the sale from the government to the British Columbia Telephone Company and not with the Canadian National Telegraphs?
I was not dealing with the Canadian National Telegraphs at the moment. I was dealing first with the British Columbia Telephone Company.

Then am I right in assuming, because I was certainly under this impression, that the hon. member was perfectly satisfied on a previous occasion, for I believe he intimated that he was satisfied with the arrangements made by the government with respect to the sale made to the British Columbia Telephone Company? Is that not a fact?

That is correct, Mr. Chairman. I indicated to the minister that I felt the outline he had given us of the sale to the British Columbia Telephone Company and the terms on which that company indicated they were going to take over government employees was quite satisfactory. But my point is that recent correspondence I have received indicates that the understanding I had formed, and I think possibly the understanding the minister had formed, of the arrangements to be made either was not correct or the undertakings are not being carried out.
I have never received any information to that effect with reference to either part of the deal.

I confess this came to my attention and I assumed it would be taken up with the minister by the telephone branch employees in the same way as a certain situation with regard to the telegraph branch employees had been.
Supply-Transport
It certainly comes to me as a surprise but I will be glad to look into it.

I am glad to hear that and I will outline the case very briefly. As regards the minister's statement at page 3310 of Hansard with reference to the arrangements for superannuation rights made with the B.C. Telephone Company, I have received this letter from one of the employees which indicates that the wages are slightly better. It indicates also that those employees who are over 45 years of age-and the figures are given as follows: two in Ashcroft, one in Alexis Creek, one in Bella Coola and all three in the Williams Lake district at the 150-Mile House; that makes a total of seven -have been asked to sign waivers of pension rights and other benefits given by the B.C. Telephone Company to their regular employees, and this is protested as being discrimination. They go on to point out that they were given no information before this deal as to what the status would be on being taken over by the B.C. Telephone Company or whether they had any choice of remaining with the civil service except that their names could, if they elected, be put on the preferred list until a vacancy occurred in the civil service.
The main point is that these employees will have lost seniority plus 18 days accumulated sick pay per year and the security of a pension when unable to work. They point out that if they sign this waiver requested by the B.C. Telephone Company they can be discarded at any time their health fails them. They also say that as far as they can learn, these conditions, that is to say the conditions that the telephone company is now asking them to accept, are included in the agreement for the sale of the government telephone and telegraph system to the new owner. They ask if some system could not have been worked out where they could contribute the same amount towards pension as they did with the government and give them an equivalent form of protection when they reach retirement age. Some of these men now over 45 years old have worked for the government system for over 20 years and now have no security for their old age; they have no choice in the matter because if they refuse to transfer to the new owner they would be unemployed while awaiting a new job in the civil service list.
I am sorry if the minister has had no previous notice of this complaint because I am sure that he and I both shared the impression that the employment arrangements with

Supply-Transport
the telephone side of the system were satisfactory. I will not go into further detail at this stage but I will send further particulars over to the minister.
I should like to get the details because I certainly would like to look into the matter.

It sounds to me as though either I had formed a misunderstanding of the nature of the agreement or possibly the agreement itself is not being fully discharged.
However, I have in addition some complaints with respect to employees on the telegraph side who have been taken over by the Canadian National Telegraphs. Here I know the minister has had these matters drawn to his attention because I have received copies of letters which have been sent to him by the employees concerned. I have drawn to his attention the cases of some of the employees and others, as I understand it, have been drawn to the attention of the minister by the amalgamated civil servants of Canada, Vancouver branch. For instance, I have here a copy of a letter to the minister dated April 12 from that branch of the amalgamated civil servants of Canada. I see that it is getting near to 10.30, Mr. Chairman, and I therefore do not wish to delay the committee by going into an excessive amount of detail. However, the position in summary is this.
The conditions accorded by the telegraph company to the employees of the government system were early discovered to be unacceptable by quite a substantial number of those employees. They made the request-and I made the suggestion on their behalf in addition-that if the conditions of service with the new owners were found to be unsatisfactory, some assurance should be given to these men that they might transfer into other parts of the government's communication system or into other branches of the civil service, because this is not a case where some extraneous act beyond the control of the government or anybody else has taken place which deprived men of their livelihood, in which case you might say that they have to take the rough with the smooth.
This is a case where the government, as a matter of policy, has decided to dispose of its system, knowing full well-it must have known it-that there were a number of long-service employees with that system who on account of their age and the fact that they had been exclusively engaged in that type of occupation would have nowhere else to go or no other field to look to for alternative employment. I cannot use any other words than these to describe the situation. I think it is unfair and callous to put these men in

the position where you are saying to them: If you do not like the terms of service offered to you by your new employers, you can shift for yourselves.
I have referred the matter, as I say, to the minister. I must say that from him I had an indication that he would give it very sympathetic consideration. I referred it to the chairman of the civil service commission and from him I understood that strenuous efforts would be made to find alternative employment for them in the civil service. So far, however, nothing has happened. I have had no word from either source since my letters of April 10; and so far as I am able to make out from complaints I have received from both Vancouver and Ashcroft, this situation has not been adjusted with respect to many of these employees. I want to make it quite clear that with respect to one individual whose case I took up, it was satisfactorily adjusted; but with respect to the others, both at Ashcroft and Vancouver, no satisfaction has been obtained.
I can only say this for these men who have never complained and who have been the finest type of government employees in small communities. In some cases they have entered fully into the community life and have been an integral part of that community. They are now pretty much disillusioned as to what it means to be turned out into the world at their age by this deal. I am going to read one paragraph from a letter of a man who served for many years. He is fairly well resigned, but he sums up the situation as follows:
Now that the dust has more or less settled, I think the important thing, over and above the importance to the employees concerned and their naturally worried state concerning their futures, has been the government's steadfast refusal to answer questions put to it by duly elected members of parliament not only in this matter, but from a perusal of Hansard in other matters too. This is truly I do think, contempt of parliament and the people of this country and is frightening in its import. What causes individual cabinet ministers to act in such a fashion, I don't know, but I for one, don't like it.
I think that paragraph summarizes the views of these men. While it might give us some satisfaction to raise hell, as it were, about the matter here I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that my concern with it goes a great deal further than that. I would not be raising the matter here if it were not for the fact that although I have written to the minister and to the chairman of the civil service commission and have asked them to do what they can to get these men alternative employment in the civil service, I have had no satisfaction from correspondence. I therefore feel bound to take this course here so

that even if eventually we get no other satisfaction for these men, they will know that they have had their case laid before the authorities and that the treatment they have received is not to go unnoticed. I hope that we shall be able to get concrete results for them, but I feel bound to raise the matter here in any event and to make the strongest possible protest against the treatment they have had. Whether the responsibility lies with the department or with the Canadian National Telegraphs, I do not know but I want to say that I feel that these men have not had a fair deal.
Mr. Chairman, may I say-

I have a little bit to add on exactly the same thing before the minister answers. Perhaps it would save time. I have also had complaints from former employees of the government telegraph service on Vancouver island who are now employees of Canadian National Telegraphs and B.C. Telephone. Their complaint consists largely in this, that many of the offices that existed under the old government telegraph scheme have now been closed. While I suppose the purchasing companies are carrying out the letter of the agreement what is actually happening in many cases is that employees with a long record in the government service, with their homes established, some in the city of Nanaimo and in other cities on Vancouver island, are being told, shall I say, that the only chance for them to continue in employment with the new employing company is to take a job at some very remote place on the island such as Alert Bay or Port Hardy, places where there is no living accommodation for them or their families.
This correspondent points out that some of these employees have had thirty years service, some even forty-three years, in the government employ and goes on to say:
Due to the superannuation act not applying to this branch until 1939 these employees have not got full pensionable credits, as this involved the paying back of a large sum of money, and the wages being low the majority of employees could not afford to do so, although some have as much as forty-two years service with the government. If the employees take their immediate pension those nearing the 60 year old mark will lose 16 per cent of their pension, which means a large drop in their pension at the present cost of living.
Would appreciate some concrete information on the salaries those employees transferring to the Canadian National Telegraphs will receive. Will they receive their former salary which they received from the government or go on the Canadian National Telegraphs rating which I understand is lower than paid by the government?
Supply-Transport
This correspondent told me when I saw him that there are quite a number who are affected in this way. They are placed in the position of having to accept employment at really impossible places for married men with families on the penalty of losing their positions entirely. I wonder whether the minister did have any undertaking with the company that these men would be given some sort of comparable employment if the offices in which they were employed were going to be closed.

I would not want hon. members of the house to think that the Department of Transport is not as much concerned about these employees as the hon. members who have spoken. There are many other hon. members who have taken up the matter either by correspondence or by verbal representations to me, and I do not want to name one rather than another because there are many. Let me deal with this matter in two ways.
In so far as the B.C. Telephone Company is concerned, I had been under the impression all along that the deal was a good one, and I am surprised that the matter raised by the hon. member for Kamloops does exist. I take it that he has received information which is accurate, and I am surprised because I never had any intimation that all the employees taken on by the B.C. Telephone Company were not satisfied with their work. However, as I said and as I undertook, I will look into the matter at the first opportunity.
Dealing with the other phase, I would remind the house that Canadian National Telegraphs is not a division of the Department of Transport but rather a division of the Canadian National Railways, and Canadian National Railways must of course take the responsibility for this matter. That does not mean that we here are not interested in the employees getting a fair deal. We are, and it was a condition of the purchase that, all things being equal, these men would be given a reasonable chance at employment under reasonable conditions. I am not using the right language. I put the terms of the agreement on the record before when I had it here, but I do not have it now.
But let me say that we are going to do our best to find employment for these people comparable to that which they had before, I have had more correspondence about these employees than any other group of employees who have, because of purchase or assignment, been put out of work. I can think of

Supply-Transport
the 260-odd radio employees of the Department of Transport who were displaced when we cancelled radio licences. We found employment for every one of them with the exception of seven, and among those there was present the question of age.
Here there are about 185 employees concerned. I think it is safe to say that in so far as the B.C. Telephone Company is concerned all of them have found work at better wages. As to the question of superannuation, I must look into it. I say that the conditions there are good with that exception, and I knew nothing about it. In so far as the Canadian National Telegraphs is concerned, I know there are a number of serious difficulties, but I believe that so far there are only eight or nine men who have been assigned to positions with which they are not satisfied and where they are being offered positions at a lower rate than they originally received.
What the total is I am not able to say, but we in the Department of Transport, together with the civil service commission, are going to do everything we can to find employment for these people. We are doing that now and because of the representations that have been made, both from this side of the house and the other side, I hope, although it may not be possible to deal with all of them because there are certain age requirements which will make it difficult to consider them all, that we will be able to do as well with the Canadian National Telegraphs operations as we did in the case of the employees of the radio branch of the department.

I know the minister is
extremely busy with this and other matters. I know that the taking over has not been easy and that he has devoted a lot of attention to it. May I ask him whether he could not instruct his officials to keep all those members who are concerned-and I want to give credit to the many other members who are equally concerned-informed? As I have pointed out, I have had this lengthy letter of April 6 summarizing the situation and I have a copy of the letter sent to the minister on April 10. I telephoned and wrote to various people, the chairman of the civil service commission and the minister, but I have had nothing since, and on the basis of that and subsequent correspondence the dissatisfaction, so far as I am aware, continues unabated.
I am glad to hear, if I understood the minister correctly, that efforts are being made to clear up quite a number of these cases and that success has been achieved with some. I would appreciate it, and I know other members would also, if we might from time to time receive reports as to the progress.

I will be glad to keep the hon. member informed as to the cases he has brought to my attention. Other cases have been brought to my attention by other members, but I do not imagine he wants to be kept informed about those.

Not individual cases, but I have this representation made on behalf of these men by the amalgamated civil servants of Canada and it refers to what appears to be certain inequities in the employment positions offered by the Canadian National Telegraphs. It contains such phrases as this:
No such unreasonable split-trick hours exist in the C.N.T. on scheduled positions.
The reason that these men are being prejudiced is that they are offered non-scheduled positions. Then there is this phrase:
When accomplished-
The reference is to certain transfers.
-as it surely would be, the positions of former government telegraph employees taken over would be wiped out. And because they are classed as non-schedule with no seniority rights-
That certainly was a feature which I understood was not present. I understood they would be given their corresponding seniority rights. It says:
And because they are classed as non-schedule with no seniority rights, they could not bid on any vacancies in the C.N.T. system proper. They would be out of employment.
When these other positions were wiped out, they would be out of employment.
I shall bring my hon. friend up to date on that.
It is now 10.30.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the hon. member for Comox-Alberni rising to speak to an item?

Yes, Mr. Chairman, I have one or two questions about item 486. I should like to discuss with the minister one or two aspects of this sale of the government telephone and telegraph which have not been discussed by previous speakers. My questions relate more to the telegraph service. I do know that there have been some views expressed particularly in connection with what is happening to the telegraphs. I have had suggestions made to me that since the sale of these facilities the Canadian National Telegraphs appear to be following a deliberate policy of withdrawal from the Vancouver island area. I feel that it would be helpful

if the minister would give us a statement as to just what former offices of the government telephone and telegraph service have been continued in operation by the Canadian National, and what former offices have been closed.
In this connection I would suggest that if, as has been suggested to me, there is a withdrawal on the part of the Canadian National from certain areas, the minister inform the committee whether this has been done in consultation with the Canadian Pacific or wh ether there has been any consideration of the maintenance of service through these channels in cases where the Canadian National is not continuing the service formerly provided by the government service.
There is one other matter upon which I feel it would be helpful if the minister gave us some information, and that is as to the particular channel through which inspection is to be continued by the government? Is that duty a function of the government's telephone and telegraph service as it presently exists or is some other agency of government going to be responsible for the inspection the minister suggested was provided for in the agreement. I would appreciate an answer to those two questions.

The answer to the hon. member's last question is that so far as inspection services are concerned, we are out of the field with reference to the facilities we have sold. We will not be providing inspectors for any of the facilities sold either to the British Columbia Telephone or Canadian National Telegraphs.

I believe the minister misunderstood my question. If I understood him correctly, when he made his statement in regard to policy he stated that the government was reserving the right to ensure that the terms of the agreement were going to be carried out by the respective companies taking over those facilities.
I am sorry, I misunderstood.
What agency of the federal government is to be responsible?

I misunderstood the hon. member. I think perhaps the microphone is placed in such a way it is difficult to catch what is being said. In answer to the hon. member's question, I would say yes. I had understood him to ask about inspection, but apparently that is not what he was interested in. He was interested in whether we still retain the right, under the agreement, to consider the terms of it, and the answer to that is yes.
Supply-Transport
With reference to the first question, I am informed that the Canadian National Telegraphs are giving service in the areas referred to by the hon. member comparable to similar localities in Canada, and that is in agreement with the conditions of sale.
